item.title: Alaska, Hawaiian announce Osaka, Tahiti in latest long-haul expansion
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Alaska, Hawaiian announce Osaka, Tahiti in latest long-haul expansion Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines have unveiled their two newest routes across the Pacific. Alaska on Tuesday announced new nonstop service from Seattle to Japan and Tahiti. - Flights to Osaka, Japan, will begin May 14. - Service to Papeete, French Polynesia, will kick off June 11. Both routes will be operated — at least to start — by Hawaiian's Airbus A330s. With these new Osaka and Tahiti flights, Alaska Air Group will have a total of four transpacific routes out of Seattle, building on the carrier's existing service to Tokyo and Seoul. And the carrier is now planning to launch four new long-haul destinations in 2027. That's after unveiling Seattle service to Paris and Athens in August. These new Pacific routes weren't entirely surprising. In recent weeks, Alaska executives had hinted that a new Asia route was coming soon. In the end, Alaska and Hawaiian flyers will have access to two additional destinations in Asia and the South Pacific. As noted, Alaska plans to deploy Hawaiian-branded A330s on the route. These are Hawaiian's standard long-haul aircraft with legacy business-class seats up front in a 2-2-2 configuration. Hawaiian is planning to give these planes nose-to-tail retrofit with new Leihoku Suites and premium economy (though those new accommodations will not be ready in time for next summer's service). Alaska, Hawaiian double down on Seattle long-haul growth Whatever the plane, these new routes to Japan and Tahiti should be welcome news for Pacific Northwest-based flyers and members of the Atmos Rewards loyalty program. Osaka is a highly popular destination in Japan, and this route will give Alaska, Hawaiian and Atmos Rewards members a direct link to the city — no need to transit through Tokyo. And Tahiti, of course, is an immensely popular vacation spot and a gateway to other destinations in the region, like Bora Bora. Hawaiian's planes will be a familiar sight in both Osaka and Papeete. The carrier has served both cities from Honolulu for years. Alaska says those routes from Hawaii will continue. But now you'll see Hawaiian planes flying to KIX and PPT from both Honolulu and Seattle. Once Alaska and Hawaiian's four newest routes from Seattle kick off in 2027, the carrier will be operating a total of nine long-haul flights from SEA. And more are coming: It's planning to offer at least 15 by 2030. When speaking last month, Alaska executives said customers should expect the new destinations to skew more heavily toward the Pacific Ocean, versus the Atlantic. "There will be a mix, obviously, between Asia and Europe," chief commercial officer Andrew Harrison said Sept. 29. "But a little bit more toward Asia." Related reading:

item.title: The Unwritten Rules of Traveling to Hong Kong—Including the Time of Year You Should Absolutely Avoid
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Pocket-sized Hong Kong packs more of a punch than its 430-square-mile size might suggest. Split into three main areasâHong Kong Island, the Kowloon Peninsula, and the New Territoriesâmade up of 18 districts, each with their own rich history, culture, architecture, and foods, there's more than enough to keep the average tourist busy for months, never mind the usual weekend trip. With more than seven million people packed into over 9,000 high-rises, efficiency is key here, and people will judge you for holding up lines, hesitating with your Octopus card, or lingering over your dim sum table while others are waiting. That said, Hong Kong people are generally kind and helpful when it comes to asking for directions. Most also speak English, which is one of the cityâs official languages. These are the unwritten rules of traveling to Hong Kong you should bookmark to seamlessly go with the flow on your next trip. An amped-up version of London's Oyster card, Hong Kong's contactless Octopus card makes getting around the city a breeze. Download the app for free or pick a physical card at the Airport Express ticket desk in the arrivals hall or any MTR subway station (the 50 Hong Kong Dollars (or around $6.50) deposit is refunded when you return the card). It can be used on every form of transport in the city, including the Peak Tram, regular trams and ferries to the Outlying Islands, such as Lamma and Cheung Chau, as well as at more than 30,000 retail outlets from convenience stores to fast food outlets, to cinemas and museums. Load up and go. Hong Kong's Mass Transit Railways system, or MTR, covers large swathes of Hong Kong Island, Kowloon, and the New Territories, but it's the double-decker buses and pocket-rocket minibuses that fill in the gapsâoften with fantastic views of the city along the way. Hop on the #6 double-decker from Central to Stanley beach, which lurches around Hong Kong Island's mountainous southern South China Sea coast (sit upstairs on the right-hand side). Or try the #94, which winds from Sai Kung Village through Hong Kong's lush UNESCO Global Geopark to Wong Shek Pier, where you can catch a scenic old wooden ferry (known as a kaito) back to Shatin to connect to the MTR line. On the subject of public transport, there are certain rules which everyone follows. Keep right on any escalators or walkways, always let passengers alight before you board, and give you up your seat to anyone in need. And while it might be fine to crack open a bag of chips or slurp a coffee in the NYC subway, eating and drinking is not allowed on any trains, trams, buses, or ferries in Hong Kongâwhich is why they're all spotlessly clean. Hong Kong is such an outdoors-y destination that it can seem like there's little to do on a rainy day but the city has two wonderful world-class museumsâthe Hong Kong Palace Museum (70 Hong Kong Dollars, or around $9), which contains hundreds of priceless treasures borrowed from the Palace Museum in Beijing, and the gigantic M+ Museum (190 Hong Kong Dollars, or around $24.25), where the focus is highly visual contemporary Asian arts. Both should be on your list to visit rain or shine. On top of that, there are dozens of fascinating little niche museums, from a British colonial-era building dedicated to tea (Flagstaff House), to the Central Star Ferry's Maritime Museum, to The Mills, which celebrates the city's textiles industryâand almost all are free to visit on Wednesdays. Served from morning until early afternoon, dim sum is the fuel that Hong Kong runs on. To beat the crowds, it's best to arrive before 12 p.m. or after 2 p.m. (try one of the world's most affordable Michelin star restaurants, Tim Ho Wan, or the 90-year old Luk Yu Teahouse). In larger establishments you might be given your own table; in smaller joints you'll be squeezed onto a bench elbow to elbow with strangers. Tea is usually included and already on the tableâtap the table with two fingers if you need a refill. Menus tend to be printed order forms with tiny photographs of each dish. Write in the amount of each dish that you desire and then wave the form in the air for a server to pick up. To pay, take your completed form to the cashier when you're leaving. The people of Hong Kong speak Cantonese, not Mandarin, which is spoken in mainland China. The colorful, highly expressive Cantonese language forms an essential part of the city's identity, so while it's unlikely that anyone will tell you off for a cheerful âNi hao,â you will definitely earn eye rolls. The traditional greeting in Hong Kongâand Macauâis, âJo sunâ in the morning, and, âNei hoâ throughout the rest of the day. Another handy phrase worth memorizing is âMmm goiâ meaning excuse me and thank you. 7. Eat at the unglamorously titled Cooked Food Centers As a result of government bureaucracy, Hong Kong's dai pai dong (street food vendors) are becoming harder and harder to find outdoors but you can still feast on fantastic authentic Cantonese dishes at the city's reasonably priced Cooked Food Centers. You'll find at least one in every district, usually attached to a fresh food market. Don't expect anything fancy. Stalls are usually arranged around communal tables with plastic stools, disposable tablecloths, and toilet rolls for serviettes. The noise is deafening and the service brusque at best, but the atmosphere is âso Hong Kongâ and the food is always packed with flavor. Java Street or Kowloon City are pretty tourist-friendly. 8. Look out for businesses in unexpected places Hong Kong has more skyscrapers than anywhere else in the world and utilizes every precious square inch of vertical real estate, so it's not unusual to find a hotel squeezed into a few floors of an office block, or a bar on the rooftop of a multi-story, or a club in the basement of a tong lau (tenement) or a high-rise full of cafÃ©s and restaurants. It can be confusing for tourists, who don't expect to find law offices, accountants, and banks sharing space with the hospitality industry, but entrances are usually signposted or have security guards who will show you the way. At first glance, Hong Kong may look like a concrete-and-glass cyberpunk vision, but it's actually surprisingly verdant, with more than 70% of the territory protected as green space. Parks and gardens are woven into every neighborhood; check out the shocking-pink Portland Street micro park spliced between tenements in Yau Ma Tei; Victoria Park in Causeway Bay; and Kowloon Park, which has a lake populated by real-life flamingos. If you really want to pass for a local, pull on your spandex, grab an umbrella (everyone's favorite sunshade), and head for the hills to take advantage of Hong Kong's hundreds of miles of sensational hiking trails. The free Hiking Trail HK app will point you in the right direction. Hong Kong consistently ranks among the world's safest cities. Violent crime and crimes against women are extremely rare; even pickpocketing is relatively uncommon. This gives residents and tourists the luxury of being able to explore Hong Kong's most intriguing neighborhoods without a hint of worry, from the Islamic, Sikh, Hindu, and Taoist temples of multi-cultural Wan Chai, to immense public housing estates in North Point, to Sham Shui Po's fabric markets and street food stalls, to ancient walled villages such as Lai Chi Wo in the New Territories. While Westerners might think of massages as an occasional treat, Hongkongers see them as an essential part of their health regime. Massage studios are littered across the cityâjust look for signs with flashing LED feetâand are usually open until at least midnight. Said to help with everything from digestion to headaches and sleep, foot reflexology is the most popular treatment. Most salons also offer other TCM (Traditional Chinese Medicine) treatments, such as ear candling and bone-setting massages. Expect to pay about $30 for a one-hour treatment at a local place. Hong Kong generally empties during the Chinese New Year celebrations (which falls according to the lunar calendar, sometime between late January and mid-February) as mainland Chinese residents head home to visit family and Hongkongers make off on holiday. In contrast, Golden Week (which starts in early October) is Hong Kong's busiest travel period and sees an enormous amount of tour groups flock to the city, filling up shopping malls and overwhelming the main tourist attractions. If you're not a fan of jam-packed streets and long lines, this time of year is best avoided. This article was originally published in CondÃ© Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: A Kayaker Put a Life Vest on Her Dog but Forgot Her Own. Luckily, Rescuers Saved the Day.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
An Estacada Fire rescuer holds Gizmo after the dog and his owner were rescued from Oregon's Clackamas River on October 16, 2026 (Photo: Courtesy Estacada Fire District) A woman and her small dog, Gizmo, were kayaking along Oregon’s Clackamas River, roughly 30 miles southeast of Portland, when their boat flipped on October 16. With water temperatures in the low 50s and a current that threatened to sweep them downstream, the pair were left stranded in the river. Of the two, only Gizmo was wearing a life jacket. Authorities have not released the woman’s name or age, but both she and Gizmo escaped without injury. Matt Aalto, a division chief with the Estacada Fire District (EFD) who oversaw the rescue, told Outside that the incident reminds paddlers—and their pets—to always wear life jackets, regardless of how comfortable they feel on the water. “It’s almost not negotiable,” Aalto said. “Especially in the Clackamas River, which can catch paddlers off guard, particularly during stretches of warm fall weather.” EFD described the incident in a statement shared to Facebook. Authorities wrote that the woman launched near Milo McIver State Park, a popular recreation area with trails, campgrounds, and river access. According to Aalto, the woman struggled to control the kayak shortly after entering the water. The kayak flipped while she was still within sight of the boat ramp, Aalto said, leaving her standing in the river with Gizmo and a boat full of water. Aalto said the woman couldn’t self-rescue, but she was able to call her mother, who then alerted emergency responders. When firefighters arrived, the woman’s father met them at the scene and pointed out a trail that led directly to her location. “The trail did open right up to where she was at,” Aalto told Outside. “That’s pretty fortunate.” Crews positioned rescuers downstream with safety ropes in case the current swept her away, according to Aalto. Firefighters then waded into waist-deep water and first retrieved Gizmo, then his owner and the flooded kayak. The entire rescue took about ten minutes. Gizmo was wearing a properly fitted life jacket with a handle, which Aalto said may have saved the small, scruffy dog’s life. “Without a life jacket, Gizmo probably wouldn’t be with us today,” Aalto told Outside. “He may have stayed afloat, but he would have definitely, most definitely gone downstream. And whether or not he would have been found is a whole other thing.” By the time Gizmo reached shore, he was OK, albeit a little cold. “He was wide awake, staring at me, and shaking, but was still very sweet,” Aalto said. “So, I put my hand out to see if he would be interested in sniffing, and he just kind of let me pet him. But you could tell that he was a chilly little dog.” Firefighters helped his owner safely to shore, and she did not require medical treatment. Fed by rain and snowmelt from the Cascade Mountains, the Clackamas can remain cold even when the air feels mild, and strong currents can overwhelm swimmers of all abilities. On October 16, air temperatures in nearby Portland reached 78 degrees Fahrenheit, while a U.S. Geological Survey monitoring station recorded the river at 53.6 degrees that morning. Some paddlers follow the Rule of 120, a guideline that uses the combined air and water temperatures to assess the need for cold-water protection. The day’s readings totaled roughly 132 degrees, above the rule’s 120-degree threshold, though the river was still cold enough to pose a risk of cold-water shock. Sudden immersion in cold water can trigger an involuntary gasp and rapid breathing, according to the National Weather Service. If someone’s head is underwater during that initial shock, they risk inhaling water and drowning. As exposure continues, the cold can impair muscle control in the hands, arms, and legs, making it increasingly difficult to grip an overturned kayak or swim to shore. These effects can develop within minutes, well before hypothermia sets in. Oregon law requires adult kayakers to carry a properly fitting, readily accessible Coast Guard-approved life jacket, though wearing one is legally required only in rougher water with moderate to difficult rapids (Class III and above). The Oregon State Marine Board recommends wearing one regardless of the conditions. The American Kennel Club (AKC) recommends on its website that dogs wear life jackets on the water, even if they are strong swimmers. A dog thrown into moving water can become exhausted or disoriented, and a properly fitted flotation device can help keep it afloat. Not all canine life jackets are created equal. The BoatUS Foundation, a national nonprofit boating-safety organization that tests canine life jackets, says on its website that owners should look for jackets with sturdy rescue handles, wide, padded straps under the belly, and a secure fit that lets the dog move comfortably. Unlike human life jackets, canine flotation devices don’t have an official Coast Guard approval standard. Paddlers should also skip using a dog leash on the water. The AKC advises against tethering dogs to kayaks or other watercraft, since they could become trapped if the boat capsizes. Aalto told Outside that pet owners should ensure their dog can respond to voice commands before taking them on the water and choosing a life jacket suited to the animal’s size and the conditions. But as Aalto noted, keeping a dog safe on moving current ultimately depends on the paddler staying upright, alert, and afloat, too. “In this case, this person did a wonderful job,” Aalto said. “She just forgot her own.”

item.title: Why do airplane seats have to be upright for takeoff and landing?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
You've finally managed to fall asleep on the plane, reclining your seat ever so slightly, and then you feel a soft tap on your shoulder. "Please return your seat to its fully upright position," the flight attendant says. The abrupt wake-up call may feel like an unnecessary nuisance, but there's an important safety reason why passengers aren't allowed to recline their seats during takeoff and landing. So much so that in the US, the rule is enforced by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), says former flight attendant Lia Ocampo. “Keeping seats upright during takeoff and landing is required for safety,” she tells Traveller. “Flight attendants make an announcement to ensure all seats are upright. They enforce this rule, and passengers must comply.” Here’s a closer look at the safety requirements behind why your airline seat must be upright for both takeoff and landing. Takeoff and landing are critical phases of flight One confusing part of the regulation is the timing of flight attendants’ requests. It can feel frustrating when you just want to settle into your seat, recline, and get cosy before pushback. So why must your seat only be upright during takeoff and landing? Although these phases of flight are short and routine, they are among the most accident-prone stages aboard an aircraft. About 20 per cent of fatal accidents occur during takeoff and the plane’s initial climb, and about 47 per cent of them occur during the final descent and landing, according to recent data from Boeing. As such, cabin crew take special precautions during these times to ensure maximum safety for everyone on board. Potential evacuations could go faster with upright seats If an incident does occur during takeoff or landing, it’s possible that hundreds of passengers will need to evacuate the plane in a matter of seconds. “A reclined seat can trap the passenger behind you during an evacuation,” Ocampo explains. “The passenger behind you has less space to get up and evacuate quickly.” Although leaning your seat back an extra inch or two might not seem like a major safety hurdle, it can make a big difference in an airline cabin that might be smoky and chaotic in the face of an emergency. “An upright seat allows for quicker evacuations, reducing the time needed to exit the aircraft,” Ocampo says. It leaves room for the brace position in an emergency In the case of a hard landing or other safety incident, flight attendants could instruct passengers to assume the brace position. In the brace position, fliers generally are instructed to bend forward at the waist and stabilise their head with their hands by leaning on the seat in front of them. This helps protect their heads and necks from flailing on harder-than-usual impact. (The positions are usually shown in the safety card in the seat pocket.) A passenger behind a reclined seat could be prevented from assuming the most ideal brace position in an emergency. “It can also increase the impact and the risk of injury,” Ocampo notes. Although it might seem irritating to sacrifice extra room in a snug economy seat by putting your seat upright, cabin crew aren’t asking you to do so in order to be a nuisance. “Remember, flight attendants are there to keep you safe, so don't make their job hard by not complying,” Ocampo says. “Following these mandated rules makes life easier and safer for everyone on the plane, especially during an emergency.” This article was originally published by Condé Nast Traveler US.

item.title: Phoenix gains new European route as Lufthansa plans Munich service for 2027
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Phoenix gains new European route as Lufthansa plans Munich service for 2027 Lufthansa is headed to the Valley of the Sun. Beginning next August, the Star Alliance carrier will launch new nonstop service from Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX) to Munich International Airport (MUC). It will mark the first time the German carrier has offered service to Arizona. This is the second nonstop U.S. route that Lufthansa has announced this week, following Monday's unveiling of the first-ever nonstop from Columbus, Ohio, to Europe. As for Lufthansa's new MUC-PHX route, the carrier will offer three weekly flights on Tuesdays, Fridays and Sundays with an Airbus A350-900 starting Aug. 3, 2027. The plane will feature 48 business class suites, 21 premium economy seats and 224 economy seats. However, that aircraft will not feature the airline's posh, new Allegris interior. Combined with other European airlines under Lufthansa's ownership umbrella, PHX brings the group's U.S. destinations to 26. Lufthansa and its peers — particularly Air France, British Airways, Iberia and KLM — have pushed into more secondary U.S. cities in recent years. The expansion is fueled by a few factors: - U.S. residents have a seemingly insatiable appetite for European travel. - There is widespread adoption of newer, fuel-efficient planes like the Airbus A321XLR and Boeing 787, which can fly profitably to smaller cities. - Certain airports offer incentives for new flights. Minneapolis, Nashville, Pittsburgh, Raleigh-Durham, St. Louis, San Diego and others have all gained new transatlantic flights as a result of this expansion. All of the major European carriers benefit from close, immunized partnerships with U.S. airlines that allow them to operate easily across the Atlantic. Air France and KLM are tied to Delta Air Lines, British Airways and Iberia are linked with American Airlines, and Lufthansa is partnered with United Airlines. American, Delta and United have also announced their own multi-route expansions to Europe for 2027. Lufthansa shifts Seattle route to Discover In addition to the new CMH and PHX routes, Lufthansa will shift its existing Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) service to its leisure subsidiary, Discover Airlines. The affected routes are SEA-MUC and SEA-Frankfurt Airport (FRA), and they are scheduled to be operated by a Discover Airbus A330. The number of flights a week remains unchanged. Discover is not a member of Star Alliance, which means loyalty benefits are not guaranteed, including for members of Lufthansa's close partner, the United MileagePlus loyalty program. item.title: A beginners guide to visiting Juneau, Alaska, by cruise ship
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
A beginners guide to visiting Juneau, Alaska, by cruise ship Most cruises stop at Juneau — for good reason. Alaska's capital has some of the widest range of attractions and shore excursions of any port in the Inside Passage. Surrounded by mountains, glaciers and the vast wilderness of Tongass National Forest, this engaging city manages to feel both wildly remote and adventure-charged despite being one of Alaska's busiest visitor destinations. A visit here can mean whale-watching, flightseeing or hiking. Numerous operators run excursions by boat or seaplane, while downtown's shops, restaurants and historic attractions are within easy walking distance from the cruise docks. Just a few miles from the port, you'll also find Mendenhall Glacier — one of North America's only true "drive-up" glaciers. Juneau offers a fascinating mass of contradictions: It's the state capital, but it's more than 500 miles from 95% of Alaska's population. It's on the North American mainland, but cut off from the rest of the country by mountains. It's the fifth-least-populous U.S. state capital, with around 31,000 year-round residents. However, it's also the largest U.S. capital in land area, at 3,250 square miles (most of which is wilderness). The stunning but logistically challenging setting imbues Juneau with a can-do spirit and a love of outdoor recreation. More than 1.5 million passengers visit here each year; a daily cap was implemented in 2026 of 16,000 passengers in port Sunday to Friday and just 12,000 on Saturday. This means Saturday is noticeably less crowded everywhere from downtown to the Goldbelt Tram and along popular trails. You'll also find shorter lines and better last-minute excursion availability on weekends, while mid-week port days remain the busiest. Since there's so much to see and do here, ships generally spend a full day in port (anywhere from eight to 13 hours). This means that even if you book a whale-watching trip, glacier tour or flightseeing adventure, you'll usually you'll likely still have enough to explore downtown and ride the Goldbelt Tram up to Mount Roberts. Here's our guide to making the most of your time in Juneau. - Sensational natural scenery, from towering mountain peaks to pristine waterways. - Endless opportunities for viewing wildlife (whales, eagles and bears, to name a few). - Plenty of top sights within walking distance of the ship docks. - Excessive crowds. Even with the passenger cap, up to five large ships dock downtown each daily during peak season. - The high cost of many shore excursions, which can feel spendy even by Alaska's standards. - Language: English. - Currency: U.S. dollar; credit cards are widely accepted. - Time zone: Juneau is on Alaska Standard Time, which is an hour behind U.S. Pacific Standard Time, and it observes daylight saving time. - Weather: Juneau sits in a temperate rainforest, and rain is common throughout the May–September cruise season. Pack layers and a waterproof jacket, even on days that start out clear. Summer temperatures typically range in the mid-50s to mid-60s. Juneau's cruise port lies along South Franklin Street, in the Gastineau Channel. Depending on where your ship berths, it's a five- to 30-minute walk to the heart of downtown. Most piers are within easy strolling distance of shops and attractions, although the AJ Dock at the southern end of the port sits about 1.5 miles away and is frequently served by shuttle buses. Taxis and share-ride services, such as Uber and Lyft, are available at the cruise docks. If you've booked a shore excursion, transportation is typically included with tour buses picking up and dropping off passengers near their ship. Downtown is compact and walkable, though several streets climb steeply from the waterfront. You can easily spend anywhere from an hour to a half day strolling downtown Juneau's historic core. The historic neighborhood is home to handsome gold rush-era buildings dating back to the late 19th and early 20th centuries; many of them contain shops and galleries that specialize in Alaskan art, crafts and keepsakes. Begin at the Juneau Visitors Center, a sleek stainless-steel building right by the ship docks. Here you can pick up free walking tour maps and hiking maps and get detailed sightseeing advice. As you stroll the tree-lined streets, keep an eye out for the 13 beautifully painted cedar totem poles crafted by Alaska Native artists. Carve out some time at the Sealaska Heritage Institute, which opened in 2016 inside a building designed as a work of Alaska Native art. Here you'll find galleries of Tlingit, Tsimshian and Haida art, an authentic Tlingit clan house and immersive cultural exhibits. A few blocks farther up Seward Street is the Juneau-Douglas City Museum, an intimate space offering deep dives into local Native culture alongside the city's boomtown gold rush history. You can also step inside the classic 1931 Alaska State Capitol building. A short walk west leads to the superb Alaska State Museum, a world-class contemporary exhibition space with collections that tell the story of Alaska's people and natural history. Keep an eye out for other notable landmarks, including the stately 1912 Alaska Governor's Mansion and the gold-domed St. Nicholas Russian Orthodox Church, built in 1893. For panoramic views, step onto the Goldbelt Tram, which whisks passengers 1,800 feet from the cruise dock up Mount Roberts. At the top, you can visit the small nature center and its wildlife displays, watch a short film on the Tlingit people, enjoy pub fare at the Timberline Bar & Grill or set out for a hike on one of many scenic hiking trails. The latter are mostly short and easy with sublime views. Established in 2017, the Juneau Seawalk is a wide, accesible boardwalk that curves along the downtown waterfront from South Franklin Street to Overstreet Park. It's lined with striking modern metal sculptures — including Tahku, a life-sized bronze humpback whale fountain — and illuminated in the evening by LED lights. Juneau's municipal boundaries stretch far beyond the city center, putting several worthwhile attractions within a 30- to 60-minute drive of the cruise docks. Although you can easily keep yourself busy downtown, renting a car or hiring a taxi can be a rewarding way to see a bit more of what this verdant community has to offer — and to venture away from the crowds. The closest attraction is the Last Chance Mining Museum, housed in a 1912 compressor building inside the former AJ Gold Mine. It's just a couple of miles from the port. Seven miles northwest of downtown, Glacier Gardens Rainforest Adventure is a lush 50-acre botanical garden known for its colorful "flower towers" — upside down trees crowned with a riot of blooms — and guided golf-cart tours through the temperate maritime rainforest. A further 5.5 miles along Glacier Spur Road is Juneau's most famous attraction: Mendenhall Glacier. The visitor center overlooks the 13-mile river of ice flowing from the Juneau Icefield while a network of well-maintained trails provides easy access to glacier viewpoints, waterfalls and wildlife. One of the more popular is the level 2-mile, round trip trail to 400-foot Nugget Falls. Continue seven miles beyond Mendenhall Glacier Visitor Center to find Auke Bay, a scoop of blue harbor and a prime viewing spot for eagles, sea lions, porpoises and whales. It's also the stepping off point for many of Juneau's whale-watching tours. For a quieter outing, the National Shrine of St. Thérèse sits on a tiny island linked by a causeway about 15-minutes from Auke Bay. Home to a 1930s stone chapel and acres of tranquil gardens, it offers a peaceful spot to stroll, meditate or admire the sea. Perhaps no Alaska port offers a more impressive variety of shore excursions, from the mild to the wild. Hiking tour or helicopter landing on Mendenhall Glacier Numerous companies offer a range of thrilling ways to experience this iconic glacier, many that add on a dog-sledding experience, salmon bake or stop at Glacier Gardens. One of the most memorable offerings is a helicopter ride over the Juneau Icefield, followed by a landing on the glacier and a short walk on the ice. Other companies offer guided hikes through the adjacent rainforest and onto the glacier, and even more spectacular treks let you go inside one of the glacier's brilliant blue-hued ice caves. Another option is a seaplane flight over several of the region's most impressive glaciers. Expect to pay around $135 to $225 for a guided hike. Helicopter landing tours are roughly $390 to $560, while combo trips that add dogsledding or ice-cave access can top $700 or more. Whale-watching excursion out of Auke Bay These enjoyable half-day cruises are offered on everything from 20-passenger research vessels to larger boats typically holding up to around 80 passengers — heated cabins and large picture windows are standard. The tours navigate a pristine habitat teeming with humpback whales, and there's also an excellent chance of seeing seals, sea lions, porpoises and myriad sea birds. The cost is usually $150 to $225 per person for a standard 3- to 4-hour whale-watching cruise. Expect to pay more for smaller boats and private charter. Seaplane excursion to Taku Glacier Lodge This relaxing trip combines stunning glacial scenery from a seaplane flight with a hearty salmon feast at a the rustic 1923 lodge in the Alaska bush. It's a great way to experience the remote locale without an arduous hike. Expect to pay $500 to $600 per person, which includes the seaplane flight and salmon feast. A fun activity for families, these low-impact tours typically entail exploring a historic underground mine and then panning afterward. You're not going to yield a great fortune in precious metals, but participants do usually find a few flecks of gold or pieces of garnet in their pan. Basic gold-panning tours start around $80 to $100 per person, while those bundled with a salmon bake or historic mine tour typically cost $100 to $150. This seven- to eight-hour excursion takes visitors into one of the Inside Passage's most spectacular fjords, where you'll view mighty North Sawyer Glaciers, as well as cascading waterfalls and majestic cliffs. Expect to pay around $330 to $375 per person. Note that unstable ice conditions can divert departures from Tracy Arm to nearby Endicott Arm to view Dawes Glacier instead, a comparable but not identical experience. Confirm with your operator before booking. Best Juneau outdoor activities near the cruise port Although many of Juneau's most popular outdoor adventures involve booking helicopter, seaplane or boat rides, there are plenty of exciting ways to experience nature on your own. Easily accessed via the Goldbelt Tram from the cruise dock, Mount Roberts is laced with trails that range from short and easy treks near the tram station to more strenuous jaunts, like the 3-mile climb up to 3,465-foot Gastineau Peak. Another rigorous option is skipping the tram ride up and hiking the steep 2-mile trail that rises from downtown to Mount Roberts. You can always return to the cruise port via the tram. The easiest and most accessible way to enjoy nature right near the port is to stroll along this art-lined boardwalk path, which offers lovely views of the waterfront. Escape the crowds near the port by heading out to this peaceful beach off Glacier Highway, about a 30-mile drive or taxi ride north of downtown. It's a quiet spot where two rivers empty into the Lynn Canal, and it features picnic tables, trails and gorgeous sunset views. It's common in summer to see humpback whales, seals, otters and sometimes even bears feasting on salmon. Near the port, Cycle Alaska rents road bikes, mountain bikes, gravel bikes and e-bikes and can recommend the best areas for a ride. The company also offers guided tours of Mendenhall Valley. Outfitters at Auke Bay Harbor rent single and double kayaks and stand-up paddleboards for use in the bay's sheltered and generally calm waters. These companies can also provide instruction and even classes for paddlers of all abilities, and they offer guided tours that include whale- and wildlife-watching. - On foot: This is a great port for walkers. Most of Juneau's shops, restaurants and museums are clustered within several blocks that begin across from the cruise ship dock. Just keep in mind that if your ship is docked at one of the berths farther from downtown, the most distant being AJ Dock (about a mile away), your walk into downtown can increase by up to a half hour. - Shuttle bus: Frequent narrated bus shuttles run from the cruise port to Mendenhall Glacier. Sightseeing trolleys also circulate through downtown. - Taxi or ride-hailing service: It's easy to hail taxis at the cruise ship port, and Juneau is served by Uber and Lyft. Fares beyond downtown can be expensive, with rates typically of at least $30 each way to Auke Bay and $45 each way to Mendenhall Glacier. - Car: This is an excellent option if you want to explore beyond downtown at your own pace, especially if you're making multiple stops. Rates during the cruise season can be steep (typically $100 to $150 for the day); for the best deals and to assure availability, try to book a few weeks before your visit. You'll find plenty of options within an easy walk of the cruise ships, both along the waterfront and a few blocks inland downtown. Expect a line at both waterfront locations of Tracy's King Crab Shack, which is justly famous for "crab in all shapes and sizes," including legs and claws with drawn butter, as well as crab bisques and cakes. Beloved for decades, The Hangar on the Wharf occupies the building in which Alaska Airlines was formed, and it doles out halibut nachos, burgers, steaks and craft beer. A convivial hangout with fresh seafood and a great wine list, Twisted Fish Company features tall windows overlooking the water and is steps from the base station of the Goldbelt Tram. It's touristy for sure, but downtown's Red Dog Saloon is a Juneau institution dating back to around 1890 — and it definitely has an "if these walls could talk" vibe. The place is packed to the rafters with memorabilia, and the kitchen serves hearty pub grub and local beers. For a casual bite amid South Franklin's retail strip, Deckhand Dave's food truck serves up exceptional ceviche, seafood tacos, fish-and-chips and oysters on the half shell. The decidedly upmarket bistro Salt presents artfully plated modern Alaskan fare and well-crafted cocktails. Beyond downtown, a few spots beckon visitors looking for a meal away from the crowds. A short drive from downtown, the famous Gold Creek Salmon Bake is a favorite of cruise passengers and perfect for a family or group of friends to feast together. It's set amid a forested plot along the Salmon River and run by the outfitter Alaska Travel Adventures, which offers a tour there from the cruise port (including shuttle transportation). Out in Mendenhall Valley, Sandbar & Grill is a friendly and less-touristy option for lunch or dinner on your way to or from the glacier. The beer-battered shrimp and halibut are good bets. And overlooking Auke Bay Harbor, the Hot Bite is a cheerfully casual stop spot for fish tacos, burgers and milkshakes, which are available in more than 30 flavors. Seafood rules the day in the Inside Passage, and Juneau has a wealth of superb purveyors of local dishes like sweet and tender Alaskan king crab and halibut fish-and-chips. You'll find wild-caught salmon on just about every menu, served in any number of formats: grilled, blackened, smoked and in tacos and chowders. Reindeer sausage is a popular local favorite, and it's usually served like a hot dog with toppings such as cheese, chili, mustard and relish. The city is home to several excellent breweries, including the state's largest purveyor, Alaska Brewing Company. The company has a tasting room and pub right by the cruise port, and its main location is a few miles northwest near Mendenhall Valley. Beautifully designed Alaska Native art and crafts are a specialty here, including Tlingit and Haida totem poles and other carvings, fiber arts, beaded jewelry and Ulu knives. The Sealaska Heritage Store is especially well regarded for Alaska Native art. Running alongside the cruise docks, South Franklin Street is lined for several blocks with colorful wood-frame 1920s and 1930s buildings that house souvenir shops and galleries stocked with the usual Alaska logo and themed apparel, wildlife photography, smoked salmon jerky and quirky gifts. One local specialty is a jewelry set with locally mined gold nuggets. Also, look for gently exfoliating soap made with silt from the area's glaciers. Walking through the downtown historic district and soaking up the views of wood-frame gold rush-era buildings set beneath the dramatic mountain peaks that rise above the city is a great way to pass your time without spending a cent. On weekday afternoons, you can take free guided tours of the State Capitol, or you can see the building on a free self-guided audio tour. You can meander along the downtown waterfront via the Juneau Seawalk, which features public art installations, including the giant whale fountain Tahku. You may even spy some of the local wildlife in and around downtown, such as bald eagles, which soar above and often land beside downtown buildings. Look out across Gastineau Channel to view harbor seals, harlequin ducks and blue herons. If you have the time and stamina to hike up to Mount Roberts instead of taking the tram, you'll pay nothing if you hike back down again. If you prefer to return by tram, the "down-only" one-way fare is just $20 (compared to $60 for an all-day ticket). Can you visit Mendenhall Glacier without booking a tour? Yes. You can visit Mendenhall Glacier on your own without booking a tour or excursion. To get there, take a taxi or direct glacier shuttle to the Mendenhall Glacier Visitor Center. There is a public bus, but it stops 1.5 miles from the visitor center. Is Juneau walkable from the cruise dock? Yes. Most shops, museums, and restaurants are within a 5- to 15-minute walk of the main cruise ship piers. How much should I budget for a day in Juneau? Walking downtown, exploring the Seawalk and visiting free sights requires little spending beyond lunch ($20 to $40). However, if you plan to book major excursions, such as whale watching, helicopter landings or fjord cruises, budget $150 to $600 or more per person. Do I need to book excursions in advance? Yes. High demand and strict capacity limits on activities such as flightseeing, helicopter tours and glacier excursions, mean popular options routinely sell out months ahead of the cruise season. For magnificent natural scenery, lively shops and top-notch dining steps from your ship — as well as a truly impressive array of shore excursions that represent the best of Alaska's Inside Passage — you can't beat Juneau as a thrilling and easy-to-navigate cruise port.

item.title: Southwest Rapid Rewards: How to earn and redeem points, elite status and more
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Southwest Rapid Rewards: How to earn and redeem points, elite status and more Southwest Airlines was long known for policies such as no change fees and complimentary checked bags. But the airline has changed significantly over the past couple of years, introducing assigned seating, checked bag fees and new fare types while expanding its international reach through a growing network of interline partners. Southwest Rapid Rewards points remain straightforward to earn and redeem, though, and the program still offers one of the most valuable airline loyalty perks around: the awesome Southwest Companion Pass. However, the program will change substantially in 2027 with renamed elite tiers, an all-new top-tier Platinum status and a new way to qualify for the Companion Pass. Here's what you need to know about the program. Southwest Rapid Rewards program overview Like Southwest Airlines itself, the Rapid Rewards frequent flyer program has amassed a loyal following. Despite not having a standard award chart or being part of a worldwide airline alliance, Rapid Rewards' promise of no blackout dates and the ability to earn Southwest's famous Companion Pass make it an excellent choice for couples, families and those with not-so-flexible schedules. Southwest adjusted award prices to make them more "variable," as opposed to tying the award price to the cash value. In our testing, we've found that depending on the date of and demand for your flight, you can get as little as 1.1 cents or as much as 1.7 cents per point in value. TPG values Rapid Rewards points at 1.25 cents per point in our October 2026 valuations, meaning 10,000 points should give you around $125 in value. Southwest Rapid Rewards points don't expire, so you don't need to maintain regular account activity to keep them. However, if you close your Rapid Rewards account, you'll lose any remaining points. Through Dec. 31, 2026, Southwest offers A-List and A-List Preferred status. These will become Silver and Gold on Jan. 1, 2027, when Southwest adds Platinum as its new top tier. To qualify for A-List status, you must fly 20 qualifying one-way Southwest flights or earn 35,000 tier qualifying points in a calendar year. For the 2026 qualification, tier qualifying points are earned primarily from qualifying revenue flights, eligible spending on select Southwest Rapid Rewards credit cards and eligible Getaways by Southwest bookings. Rapid Rewards partner points (other than tier qualifying points earned on eligible Southwest credit cards), transferred points, purchased points, enrollment points, reward flights, Companion Pass travel and most bonus points, including tier bonus points, flight bonus points and credit card welcome bonuses, don't count toward A-List or A-List Preferred qualification. Members now earn tier qualifying points on the cash portion of flights booked using Southwest's Cash + Points option. You can also earn: The information for the Southwest Rapid Rewards Premier Credit Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, every Southwest Rapid Rewards credit card, including those that don't currently earn tier qualifying points, will instead earn 1 tier qualifying point per dollar spent on eligible purchases, with no cap on how many you can earn. With Southwest A-List status, you'll get the following: - Complimentary preferred or standard seat at the time of booking; choose an extra-legroom seat within 48 hours of departure for no additional cost (if available) - A 25% bonus on points earned from paid flights - Complimentary same-day standby, even on Basic fares (taxes and fees may apply) - Priority check-in and security lane access - Access to a dedicated A-List member phone line A-List Preferred status requires you to fly 40 qualifying one-way Southwest flights or earn 70,000 tier qualifying points in a calendar year. You'll receive all the benefits of A-List status, as well as: - Complimentary seat selection at the time of booking, including extra-legroom seats - A 100% bonus on points earned from paid flights - Two complimentary premium drinks on select flights over 250 miles Southwest Silver, Gold and Platinum status in 2027 In 2027, Rapid Rewards elite status will change both in how it is earned and the benefits, as follows: A-List and A-List Preferred members automatically become Silver and Gold on Jan. 1, 2027, and keep that status through Dec. 31, 2027. Southwest adds Milestone Rewards at 20,000 tier qualifying points or 15 flights (choose 2,000 Rapid Rewards points or two preferred seat certificates) and 95,000 tier qualifying points or 75 flights (earn three Companion Pass trips). Earning toward the new Milestone Rewards starts Jan. 1, 2027, when tier qualifying points reset; 2026 activity does not carry over. Each companion trip can be one-way or round-trip, with taxes and fees from $5.60 one-way. Each redemption uses one full trip, even for a one-way journey (so it's best to use it for a round-trip, if you can), and Milestone Rewards earned in 2027 expire Dec. 31, 2028. In 2027, primary cardmembers who reach 130,000 tier qualifying points receive a one-time boost of 10,000 tier qualifying points toward Platinum status. Southwest also expects its first Southwest Icon Lounges to open in late 2027 at Austin-Bergstrom International Airport (AUS), Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI), Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL) in Honolulu and Nashville International Airport (BNA). A new premium Chase-issued Southwest credit card, launching in 2027, will provide lounge access; its name, annual fee and exact launch date haven't been announced. Southwest also plans to equip its fleet with Starlink Wi-Fi by fall 2027, with complimentary access for Rapid Rewards members where available. How to earn Southwest Rapid Rewards points There are a few ways to earn Southwest Rapid Rewards points — and some don't even require flying. You can earn Rapid Rewards points every time you fly on a paid Southwest Airlines flight. The number of points you'll earn depends on the cost of your flight, your elite status, the type of ticket and your payment method. Under Southwest's current fare structure, Basic fares earn 2 points per dollar spent on the base fare; Choice fares earn 6 points per dollar; Choice Preferred fares earn 10 points per dollar; and Choice Extra fares earn 14 points per dollar. A-List members receive a 25% bonus on qualifying flight earnings, while A-List Preferred members receive a 100% bonus. You can also earn Rapid Rewards points on Southwest-operated flights booked through Icelandair, Southwest's first international airline partner, as long as you add your Rapid Rewards number to the booking. These points count toward A-List and Companion Pass qualification. In 2027, Basic and Choice fares will still earn 2 and 6 points per dollar spent, respectively; Choice Preferred fares will fall to 8 points per dollar spent, and Choice Extra fares will drop to 10 points per dollar spent. Silver, Gold and Platinum members will earn 40%, 60% and 120% flight bonuses. Members transitioning to Gold from 2026 A-List Preferred status retain the 100% bonus through 2027. Beginning in spring 2027, members will also be able to redeem Rapid Rewards points directly for travel with partner airline Icelandair, as well as earn and redeem on China Airlines and Etihad Airways. Southwest has not disclosed award pricing, booking rules or whether partner flights will provide elite status credit. Southwest Airlines has several cobranded credit cards issued by Chase. - Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (see rates and fees): Earn 50,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. - Southwest Rapid Rewards Premier Credit Card: Earn 55,000 bonus points after spending $1,500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. - Southwest Rapid Rewards Priority Credit Card: Earn 60,000 bonus points after spending $2,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Southwest also offers the following business cards: - Southwest Rapid Rewards Premier Business Credit Card: Earn 80,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. - Southwest Rapid Rewards Performance Business Credit Card: Earn 80,000 bonus points after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Southwest and Chase also plan to launch a new premium Southwest credit card in 2027 that will provide access to a new network of Southwest Icon Lounges, with the first lounges expected to open by the end of 2027. Transfer points to Southwest Rapid Rewards Additionally, you can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points and Bilt Points to Southwest Rapid Rewards at a 1:1 ratio. You can transfer certain hotel points to Rapid Rewards, though they aren't usually a great value. Marriott Bonvoy transfers at a 3:1 ratio, with 5,000 bonus Rapid Rewards points for every 60,000 Marriott points transferred. With Best Western Rewards, transferring 5,000 points nets you 1,200 Rapid Rewards points. Transferring 6,000 Choice Privileges points gets you 1,800 Rapid Rewards points. And for World of Hyatt transfers, 5,000 World of Hyatt points become 2,400 Rapid Rewards points, with 50,000 Hyatt points producing 30,000 Southwest points after a 6,000-point bonus. Remember that these transfers don't earn tier qualifying points or count toward Companion Pass qualification. Other ways to earn Rapid Rewards points include via Rapid Rewards Dining and Rapid Rewards Shopping purchases, booking stays through Southwest Hotels and making purchases with other partners. Check out our overall guide on the different ways you can earn Southwest Rapid Rewards points to learn more. You can also purchase Rapid Rewards points directly from Southwest if you need to top off your account for an award. The minimum purchase is 2,000 points, and Southwest currently allows you to buy up to 60,000 points per day for yourself or as a gift. Points usually cost 3 cents each, though the program runs promotions from time to time to reduce this price. Purchased points don't count toward A-List, A-List Preferred or Companion Pass qualification. How to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points There are several ways to redeem your points, but right now, you'll almost always get the most value by using them for travel on Southwest flights. Other redemption options, like gift cards and merchandise, yield much less value. From November 2026, you can also redeem points for rental cars with Southwest's car rental partners. Later in 2027, you'll be able to use points to select seats on Southwest-operated flights, including extra-legroom and preferred seats. The process for redeeming Rapid Rewards points for flights is largely the same as booking a paid flight. Head to the Southwest homepage, enter your search criteria and select the "Points" option. Click the yellow search button to see your flight options. You'll see award pricing to the right of each available flight. You can filter flights by the number of layovers and departure times using the buttons at the top of the page. Then, click the ticket price for your desired flight and follow the onscreen prompts to book. Which fare type should I choose? You can redeem points for flights in any of the four Southwest fare types. The least-expensive option, Basic, is a good value for many travelers, though it's restrictive. Standard seats are generally assigned at check-in unless your elite status or an eligible Southwest credit card provides earlier seat selection. Cash Basic fares are nonrefundable outside Southwest's 24-hour cancellation policy, so canceling one gets you a flight credit rather than a refund. Flight changes require you to upgrade to Choice, Choice Preferred or Choice Extra first. Choice fares are slightly more flexible, with free same-day confirmed changes and standby. Additionally, if you need to cancel your flight, flight credits can be transferred to another person. But the real benefit is that you'll be able to pick a standard seat when booking your flight. Choice Preferred adds preferred seat selection, earlier boarding, expedited check-in and security at select airports, and refundable fares. Extra-legroom seats aren't included unless a separate elite status or credit card benefit provides them. Choice Extra fares are the most expensive, offering two main added benefits: complimentary extra-legroom seats at the time of booking and two free checked bags. They also include Group 1 boarding, and you'll receive one complimentary premium drink on board (on select flights over 250 miles). Basic flight credits expire after six months and are nontransferable. Credits from Choice, Choice Preferred and Choice Extra expire after 12 months and can be transferred once between Rapid Rewards members. Choice Preferred and Choice Extra cash fares can be refunded to the original payment method if canceled at least 10 minutes before departure. Southwest cardholders get their first checked bag free on each of the airline's cards. This benefit applies to the primary cardholder and up to eight travelers on the same reservation but not to flights booked with a partner airline. All cardholders can also select a seat in some capacity, even if they're flying on a Basic fare. Can I change Southwest award tickets without a fee? You can cancel Southwest award tickets without a cancellation fee, provided you meet the applicable cancellation deadline. Choice, Choice Preferred and Choice Extra fares can also be changed without a change fee. If your new award costs more, you'll pay the difference in points. If it costs less, Southwest will return the points difference to your account. Basic fares are an exception: To change a Basic booking, you must first upgrade the fare to Choice, Choice Preferred or Choice Extra. Alternatively, you can cancel the Basic award and rebook, subject to Southwest's cancellation and no-show rules. Do I have to pay taxes and fees on award tickets? You must pay certain taxes and fees when booking Southwest award tickets, starting at $5.60 one-way. If you cancel your award flight at least 10 minutes before departure, your Rapid Rewards points will be returned to your account. Eligible taxes and fees can generally be refunded to the original payment method or retained as a flight credit, depending on how they were paid. For more details, check out our guide on how to redeem your Southwest points. How can I get the most value from my Rapid Rewards points? Because Southwest's award prices vary, flexibility can help you reduce the number of points needed for a flight. One useful starting point is Southwest's Low Fare Calendar, which displays the lowest available fare for each day across a month. If your dates are flexible, compare nearby travel days before booking. After booking, keep checking the award price. For Choice, Choice Preferred and Choice Extra fares, if the price falls, you can change to the lower-priced fare and have the difference in points returned to your Rapid Rewards account. Basic award fares can't simply be changed, but you can cancel and rebook if the fare rules allow. Finally, the Companion Pass (described below) can be the biggest way to stretch your Rapid Rewards points. How much are the fees on Southwest Rapid Rewards tickets? For U.S. mainland travel booked, ticketed or changed on or after April 9, 2026, Basic, Choice and Choice Preferred travelers generally pay $45 for the first checked bag and $55 for the second each way. Southwest cardholders and up to eight passengers on the same reservation get the first bag included. A-List members pay $35 for the second; A-List Preferred and Choice Extra travelers get two included. Silver members transitioning from 2026 A-List qualification retain the $35 second-bag rate through 2027. Hawaii interisland, oversized and overweight baggage fees differ. Southwest doesn't charge change or cancellation fees, but you'll pay any fare or points difference. A no-show can cause you to forfeit funds or points. Maximize your points with the Southwest Companion Pass The Southwest Companion Pass is undoubtedly one of the most valuable perks of the Rapid Rewards program. After earning the pass, you can choose a companion to travel with you for just the cost of taxes and fees on eligible Southwest-operated flights booked directly through Southwest, subject to seat availability. You can use the Companion Pass on as many flights as you'd like, effectively doubling the value of your Rapid Rewards points. Through Dec. 31, you can earn a Companion Pass with 100 qualifying one-way segments or 135,000 Companion Pass qualifying points in a calendar year. Eligible points include those from paid Southwest flights, Southwest credit card welcome bonuses and purchases, the Southwest debit card and base points from partners such as hotels, car rentals, Rapid Rewards Dining and Rapid Rewards Shopping. Partner bonus points and transfers from Chase Ultimate Rewards, Bilt and hotel programs don't count. You can only designate one companion at a time, but you can change your companion three times per calendar year. You can change your companion through your Southwest account, but you'll need to cancel any existing reservations that include your current companion first. According to the airline, allow up to 48 hours for the change to take effect, but in our experience, it happens immediately. Remember that your companion will not earn Rapid Rewards points on their flight, but you will still earn points if you fly on a paid ticket. Your Companion Pass earned under the 2026 rules will be valid for the remainder of the year in which it's earned and the entirety of the following year (unless you earn the pass through a special promotion). Starting in 2027, Companion Pass qualifying points will be retired. Members can earn three Companion Pass trips at 95,000 tier qualifying points or 75 flights, while Platinum status at 140,000 tier qualifying points or 100 flights provides unlimited trips. Existing Companion Pass holders will retain unlimited use through the original end of their term. Starting in 2027, credit card welcome and referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus-category points and hotel or rental car partner earnings will no longer count toward Companion Pass qualification. Southwest says bonuses on cards approved by Dec. 2, 2026, can still count if the spending requirement is met in early 2027. Southwest Rapid Rewards points are easy to earn and redeem, and the incredibly valuable Companion Pass sets Southwest apart from other airlines. Don't miss your fast track to a Companion Pass with the right cobranded credit card in 2026. However, Rapid Rewards will undergo substantial changes in 2027. Every Southwest credit card will help members earn status; Milestone Rewards will provide earlier benefits; Platinum will make the Companion Pass a formal top-tier benefit; and international partners will expand award options. On the downside, credit card welcome bonuses will generally stop counting toward Companion Pass qualification. Choice Preferred and Choice Extra will earn fewer points, Silver and Gold will require more qualifying flights and Gold members will earn a smaller flight bonus than A-List Preferred members currently do. Terms & restrictions apply. See rates & fees.

item.title: Bilt adds JetBlue TrueBlue as a 1:1 transfer partner
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Bilt adds JetBlue TrueBlue as a 1:1 transfer partner Bilt just added JetBlue TrueBlue as its 27th transfer partner, calling it "one of the most requested transfer partners" among its members. Now, Bilt members can transfer points to JetBlue TrueBlue at a 1:1 ratio via the Bilt app or website once they link their TrueBlue account with their Bilt account. You can transfer in increments of 1,000 points, so every 1,000 Bilt Points that you transfer to JetBlue becomes 1,000 TrueBlue points. Bilt Blue members must transfer at least 2,000 points per transfer, while other Bilt members must transfer at least 1,000 points per transfer. Bilt says "transfers will complete almost instantly," so you can transfer shortly before redeeming TrueBlue points for an award flight. Interestingly, this news comes less than a week after Rove added JetBlue TrueBlue as a transfer partner. Now you can transfer the following transferable rewards to JetBlue TrueBlue: - American Express Membership Rewards points: 5:4 ratio - Chase Ultimate Rewards points: 1:1 ratio - Citi ThankYou Rewards points: Up to 1:1 ratio (depending on your card) Bilt's 1:1 transfer ratio matches the best standard ratio offered by several other transferable rewards programs. However, Rove is offering a 20% bonus on eligible transfers to JetBlue through Nov. 14, temporarily giving members 1,200 TrueBlue points for every 1,000 Rove miles transferred. JetBlue TrueBlue uses a dynamic award pricing model for its own flights. You can redeem TrueBlue points for any JetBlue-operated flight, although the number of points required generally tracks the paid fare. In the above example, you could book a main standard seat for $149 or 10,400 points plus $5.60. This would give you a redemption rate of 1.38 cents per point, which is typical. However, that doesn't necessarily make JetBlue the best use of Bilt points. TPG's October 2026 valuations peg Bilt points at 2.2 cents each and JetBlue points at 1.35 cents each, so this transfer option may be most useful when you need to top off your TrueBlue account or find an especially valuable partner award. You can redeem JetBlue points for flights on select partner airlines, including United Airlines, Qatar Airways and Etihad Airways. Unlike awards on JetBlue-operated flights, partner award prices don't necessarily track the cash fare. JetBlue doesn't publish an award chart for these redemptions, so you'll need to search your origin and destination to see available flights and pricing. A Bilt spokesperson said that the company is "looking forward to doing more and more with TrueBlue and JetBlue in the Bilt neighborhood ecosystem over the coming months." That could lead to future promotions, such as a Rent Day transfer bonus or a Mosaic status match challenge. JetBlue is a useful addition to Bilt's already strong transfer-partner lineup, and the 1:1 ratio matches the best standard transfer ratio offered by other rewards programs. Still, TPG's October 2026 valuations peg Bilt points at 2.2 cents each and JetBlue points at 1.35 cents each. So, this option will be most useful when you need to top off your TrueBlue balance or find a valuable JetBlue or partner award.

item.title: How to Deal with a Damp Tent Without Sitting in Camp Waiting for it to Dry
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
I like to leave camp fast in the morning. I have a hard time lingering with the day’s miles hanging over my head, so I usually pack up and zip out bright and early. I can always sit around later in the day, after all, and if I have a lot of miles to put away, I don’t have time for a leisurely breakfast anyway. On many of those mornings, my tent is soggy from condensation or overnight rain. If I’m feeling lazy, the whole sodden mess goes into my pack as I pledge to myself that I’ll deal with it later. While it’s not the end of the world to unpack a still-damp tent at camp, there are ways to mitigate the mess. Not only is this more comfortable, but it’s also better for your tent’s longevity and can prevent mildew and odor buildup. Here’s how I’ve learned to keep my tent as dry as possible while maximizing efficiency during longer trail days. It’s kind of cheating to make this the first tip, but it’s pertinent, especially if you’re camping somewhere without precipitation but with potential condensation buildup. If you can, avoid camping in enclosed spaces surrounded by tall grass, in low points of gullies or valleys, or near water. All of these tent-pitching locations increase condensation buildup thanks to the higher humidity and increased ground condensation. Airflow is also important: If your tent has vents and weather allows, prop them open overnight or keep your fly partially open. This will help prevent condensation buildup inside your tent. You can exponentially speed up the drying rate by absorbing water droplets before you fold it up. Grab a buddy, hang onto all four corners, and snap the tent as hard as you can like you’re a fourth grader playing with the giant parachute in gym class. The more water you shake off before strapping it to your pack or stuffing it inside, the less you’ll have to deal with later. Plus, it’s kind of fun to see the water drops fly off. Once you snap the tent out, you can take care of water in the corners or particularly soggy spots by wiping them down with a camp towel. (I try to hit any muddy spots here, which can help prevent material degradation from dirt and abrasion. It also makes it less gross to climb into that night.) If I don’t have a microfiber cloth, I wipe my tent out with an old sock (sorry), which is better than nothing. It’s not often I choose to sit in the wind on purpose, but if I stuffed a soggy tent into my pack in the morning, I’m going to seek out an open, breezy spot to shake it out. My main stop during the day is lunch, so if my tent was wet in the morning, I try to time my lunch break for peak warmth and sun height. As soon as I stop, I take the tent out of my pack and lay it flat out while I eat. Anchor the corners so it doesn’t blow away; I also recommend adjusting it for best sun exposure and airflow as each section dries. This works best if you drape the material over brush, branches, or across taller rocks to maximize airflow, and don’t forget to shake it every now and again to clear actual water drops as they condense, which speeds up the process. This isn’t as efficient as spreading the whole thing out during a lunch break on a breezy hillside, but on days where I don’t plan to stop as much—or the sun is particularly hot—I fold the fly into a large square to maximize surface area, then attach it under the Y-straps on the top of my pack, draping it down the back to catch as much moving air as possible. Every time I stop for water, I flip the tent fabric over to expose more of it to the sun and air. Since I don’t sit around camp in the morning, I often finish my miles earlier and sit around camp in the evening. This is entirely personal preference, but it also gives me time to get the tent dry while the air is still warm and the sun is still up. Instead of flopping down immediately and elevating my feet, I set up my tent and shift it around for the best sun exposure as soon as I get to camp. On days when elevating my feet simply cannot wait, I drape the tent body and fly across branches or sturdy bushes and let the dry air do its thing.

item.title: The ‘Tavern-Style’ Pizza Takeover
item.description:
Source: Eater
In the suburbs of Chicago where they both grew up, it was just pizza, according to Brittany and Brennan Grosvenor, the couple behind Proof in Portland, Oregon. Ordering came down to the question of “thin-crust, deep-dish, or double-dough,” Brittany recalls of her family’s Friday night tradition. The Grosvernors sell the former at Proof, though the language of “thin crust” has given way to the more nationally familiar phrasing of “tavern-style,” the pizza trend that has swept from coast to coast in recent years. It’s the year of the tavern — and that means pizza style, too Outsiders might associate Chicago with its famous, tourist-beckoning deep-dish pizza, but Brittany says that’s just not reflective of reality, citing deep dish as a much less frequent treat than the Midwestern, thin-crust style that’s gaining popularity. “The pizza you get every week, or if you go to a kid’s birthday party, it’s always tavern-style,” she says. “Tavern-style” pizza — which is prevalent across the Midwest, with Chicago, Milwaukee, Minnesota, and St. Louis touting similar pies — is known for its thin, cracker-like crust, cut into a lattice instead of triangular slices. Depending on the region and the pizza shop where one’s nostalgia lies, the sauce might lean sweet or spicy. Lightness and crispness, though, is the style’s unique sell. Writing for Esquire in 2023, Omar Mamoon called the variant, which was then still on the rise, “a foil” to famously thick Detroit-style pizza, which had its big moment in the late 2010s. The beauty of the tavern-style pie is its shareability. A pizza yields more slices when cut into a grid than into triangles, explains Bradley Shorten, who’s behind both Kim’s Uncle Pizza in his hometown Chicago suburb of Westmont, Illinois, and the recently opened La Merna in Washington, D.C. Pizza cut into little squares makes for great drinking food, especially since it fits on a cocktail napkin. What makes a good pie, according to Shorten, is that every square has a little of every ingredient; the toppings go to the edge. And while the four, small corner slices might not be the “best” ones, Shorten says, they’re the ones “everybody goes for,” especially if they’re from Chicago. Over the past few years, as “taverns” have become growing fixations for a cadre of restaurateurs, the “party cut” pizza and tavern-style pizza spots have also become ubiquitous, with openings like Keepers in New York city; One Trick Pony in Forth Worth, Texas; Tillie’s Tavern Pizza in Wheat Ridge, Colorado; and Zarella and Dimmi Dimmi Corner Italian in Chicago, where the style has always been abundant. For some Chicagoans, these openings across the country are an opportunity to correct the record about their city’s pizza culture, and for other Midwesterners to claim their stake in the region’s pizza, too. When Mike Fadem opened the second location of his popular NYC pizzeria Ops — known for its wood-fired Neapolitan-esque pies with leopard-spotted crusts and pliant dough — he wanted to offer something new. Fadem is from St. Louis, where the city’s namesake pizza is super-thin. Despite his love for it, “it’s maybe not the best version of tavern pizza,” Fadem admits, noting the iteration’s many critics, some of whom take issue with its use of the gooey processed cheese called provel. The trajectory of tavern-style pizza has been like a game of telephone, he explains: St. Louis pizza is derived from thin-crust Chicago pizza, which itself came from Neapolitan pizza. Divergence has accompanied each jump. One of Fadem’s employees at Ops, meanwhile, is from New Jersey, which claims its own thin-crust, tavern- or bar-style pizza tradition. (The bar pies of the Boston area also have their own devoted following.) Accordingly, “I had this interest in ‘can we make an Ops version of this?’” Fadem says. With Ops known for sourdough, Fadem also wanted to highlight the rich flavor of whole grains. And he wanted it to be really crispy, a quality he says draws in New Yorkers. Fadem’s take is on the menu as the regionally agnostic “tavernetta.” Though St. Louis and New Jersey served as initial inspiration, the best pizza from his research was actually in Milwaukee. The Tavernetta hasn’t displaced the other pies at the restaurant; it’s ordered in addition to them, with most groups getting at least one. In June, Los Angeles cocktail spot Bar Next Door celebrated its third anniversary by adding food to its menu. Previously, the bar had allowed customers to bring in pies from Prince Street Pizza next door since Prince Street co-owner Lawrence Longo is a partner in it. “But, you know, after having a slice, sometimes you get a little full and you’re like, I want to go to bed,” says owner and bar director Brynn Smith. “That’s the whole goal for us: for people to stay a little longer, drink more. We thought the tavern-style pizza would be perfect.” The fact that the pizzas — they’re technically listed on the menu as “bar pies,” to better go with the establishment’s name — are made exclusively for the bar by Prince Street just adds another reason for people to go out, Smith says. The idea of the tavern as a social and convivial space is inseparable from the tavern-style pizza. Shorten’s goal with La Merna — which he runs with his wife Meg Schmitt, who grew up in St. Louis — was the feel of a Chicago dive bar or a Wisconsin supper club: a place with wood-paneled walls and checkered floors, where people could slide into a red leather booth for pitchers of beer and pizza and hang out for a while. As my colleague Francky Knapp wrote last year, the rising appeal of the “tavern” vibe across restaurants nationwide is rooted in the sense of providing somewhere homey and lived-in. At taverns, diners are beckoned to sprawl out and stay awhile; to free themselves of pretense and to tap into something welcoming in its familiarity. This, for so many people, is exemplified by the archetype of hometown pizza shop, which is forever tethered in our cultural imaginations to the trappings of a previous, simpler era. It’s for this reason that, in Oregon, the Grosvenors have started serving their take on Bosco sticks, the stuffed breadsticks of Midwestern cafeterias, and Italian beef with giardiniera. While they could find certain Midwestern hits around Portland, it sometimes frustrated them that they couldn’t find everything in one place. According to Brennan Grosvenor, “We’re just trying to embody the feeling: If you went into a tavern in Chicago, what could you order there?”

item.title: In Her Sequel to 'Big Little Lies,' Liane Moriarty Shines a Light on Suburban Australia's Dark Side
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Bestselling novelist Liane Moriarty recently returned to the Australian beachside setting of perhaps her best-known book, Big Little Liesâlater adapted for television by HBO in a series starring Nicole Kidman, Reese Witherspoon, Alexander Skarsgard, and Meryl Streep, among othersâfor her first sequel, Big Little Truths. In it, we rejoin the characters of this not-so-sleepy coastal community 10 years later, as they grapple both with more dark intrigue and the challenge of parenting teenagers. Moriarty took some time during the bookâs tour to tell us about the role destinations play in her work, how the television seriesâ vision of her book affected the sequel, and her top Sydney spots for writing and retreating. âI don't actually think a sense of place is one of my strengths. I find dialogue and character come easily to me, but I'm not somebody who describes scenery particularly well, and I have a very poor memory about anywhere that I've visited. I remember the people that I meet, but I find it hard to remember the actual places, which is why I always set all my books in AustraliaâI can literally look out the window and see where I am! But it's interesting to me that even if I've just written a few lines, readers can create a whole picture in their head thatâs maybe not necessarily in mine. I love thatâit's my imagination working in tandem with theirs. There's not one particular beach that the Pirriwee Peninsula in Big Little Lies and Big Little Truths is based on, for exampleâbut a lot of people think that itâs Avalon Beach, north of Sydney. I describe these two giant pine trees, which are also in Avalon Beachâthe surfers climb them to see the surfâand people are so adamant that this is where this is. My second novel, The Last Anniversary, was set on a small island on the Hawkesbury River in New South Wales. I visited an island called Ganga Island, and then I created a fictional island called Scribbly Gum Island, which I know people have actually looked up and contacted the tourism board in Sydney to find out how to get there. I like that the places take on a life outside of my books, like people almost want them to exist so they can go and visit them. I'm always interested, in the same way that Agatha Christie always wanted to put her characters in an enclosed setting, in putting my characters in small beachside or island communities. For Big Little Lies, I was really interested in those beachside communities where people from all walks of life live. It seemed very particular to them that you can have really wealthy people and also people who are struggling financially and who don't have huge homes with water views, and I just love the fact that they're all suddenly coming together at the local school. It is true to life and the northern beaches of Sydney where I have lived. I use the term âinsular peninsula,â because theyâre such beautiful places to live that people joke that, especially if they work in the area, they just never leave. They put the HBO TV adaptation of Big Little Lies in Monterey in California. I was pleased that it was still a coastal town.
