I wouldn't have liked it if it was suddenly in the Alps, that would have felt wrong. But it was close enough to my town, although I think in the HBO version everybody had a lot more money! There were a lot of beautiful, amazing homes, whereas for me, I really wanted the contrast, so I only had Celeste having a beautiful home. When I wrote Big Little Truths, I talked in the authorâs note at the beginning about how I had to give some of the charactersâfor example, the character of Renata, who was played so magnificently by Laura Dernâa bigger role in this book as a result. But the Californian setting did not affect my writing of the sequel at all; I was back in the Pirriwee Peninsula. With Nine Perfect Strangers, even though it was set in California they actually filmed it in Byron Bay, so I got to visit the set. Some viewers can tell that it's filmed in Australia, because they can hear some of the birdlife. But I think that California is similar enough to my settings that they can get away with it. Definitely with Big Little Lies and Big Little Truths, the lives of these characters seem amazing, but when you dig deeper there are all these threats. I'm always interested in characters who look like they've got it all together and perhaps they don't, and how real people present themselves to the world versus what's really going on. If you've ever developed a friendship, you might have an instant first impression and then as you get to know them, you realize, oh, actually, they're this sort of person. And in the same way it's interesting to have a really beautiful setting and then explore the dark things that can happen behind closed doors. One of my favorite authors is Anne Tyler, and she sets all her books in Baltimore. I always thought that she gave me permission to therefore set all my books in Sydney. Unless as my children got older, I could go and live on a Greek island for six months and set the book there! But I bet I would still set it as an Australian doing exactly that; I'd be seeing it through an Australian character's eyes. Because I feel like I'd need to live somewhere for a really long time to be able to write from the perspective of somebody who lived there all their lives. But a Greek island does sound pretty niceâI went to Santorini in my 20s, a really long time ago now, and I can still see the blue of that water. Everywhere I go, I want to go back to. Just before Covid I did a Scandinavian book tour, and then my family came over and met me, and we went around and did all those countries again. But usually I tend to just write in my home office. I've got two sisters who are authors and both of them like to go to cafÃ©s and write on their laptops. My sister, the author Jacqueline Moriarty, works in a particularly beautiful chocolate shop, which is also a cafÃ© and looks really magical, and her books often do have a magical side to them. But for me, the only thing I do is go to Hobart in Tasmania, where my husband's from. I like to go there to write and actually I did set some of Here One Moment there. I got out of Sydney, briefly! Because Hobart is the only place I've spent enough time to feel that I could do that. Thereâs a bit of a writing community in Hobart, and I heard one author saying she thinks there are stories in the water there. But I just love it because it's a really peaceful place to write.â Favorite district: âI love anywhere around the harbor; the botanical gardens are a beautiful place to go. Every summer in January they have an outdoor cinema; the screen comes up out of the harbor, and to sit there and see the lights and watch a movie and have a cocktail with your friends, we always say, âwhy would you live anywhere else?ââ Best beaches: âAnywhere along the northern beaches. We grew up going to Avonka Beach, which is about an hour north of Sydney. In Here One Moment I talked about going camping near Boca Beach, and Balmoral Beach closer to the city is another favorite. â Best spa or retreat: âI went to one in the north of Sydney called the Golden Door when I was researching Nine Perfect Strangers. Itâs in a beautiful bush setting, but they do not offer hallucinogens like in the book!â Favorite hotel: âThe Shangri-La in Sydney is a wonderful place to stay, with beautiful views of the harbor.â Best coffee spot: âWe're very proud of our coffee in Sydney, and so we make a big deal of itâI always feel like whenever I go overseas, I'm just meeting fellow Australians complaining about the coffee. Kirribilli is a lovely place to get coffee, on the harbor with views of the opera house.â This article was originally published on CondÃ© Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: Amex Business Platinum adds coworking access and a new $500 credit
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Amex Business Platinum adds coworking access and a new $500 credit American Express is adding a benefit that could save some business cardmembers money on coworking spaces. Starting Oct. 22, eligible U.S. cardmembers with The Business Platinum Card® from American Express or the American Express® Corporate Platinum Card will receive a complimentary ZO membership from Tishman Speyer. The membership includes unlimited access to participating ZO Clubhouses, four Studio coworking day passes per month and up to $500 in annual statement credits toward eligible event space bookings or a Dining Club membership. More than 25 participating Clubhouse and Studio spaces are located in Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles, New York City, San Francisco and Washington, D.C. This isn't the Business Platinum's first coworking benefit. The card previously offered complimentary WeWork membership, introduced in 2019, with access ending in 2020. The ZO partnership brings coworking access back to the card, though with a smaller footprint and different access rules. Here's how the benefit works and who could get the most value from it. The information for the American Express Corporate Platinum Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. What are ZO Clubhouses and Studios? The membership gives you access to two types of spaces operated by Tishman Speyer. ZO Clubhouses are lounges where you can work, meet someone or take a break. Amenities vary by location, but some offer dining and events alongside places to work and relax. Studio offers a more traditional coworking setup, with shared desks, private offices and meeting rooms, along with amenities such as high-speed Wi-Fi and complimentary coffee and tea. Event spaces are also available to book separately. Eligible cardmembers receive unlimited access to participating Clubhouses, plus four Clubhouse guest day passes per week. Studio access is limited to four complimentary day passes per month. At The Spiral in Manhattan's Hudson Yards, the Clubhouse is on the 66th floor, with skyline views and dining from Café Llama. Studio occupies lower floors in the same building. Keep in mind that membership doesn't cover every expense — dining, private spaces and certain experiences cost extra. How much value does the benefit offer? It's easiest to see the value in the Studio day passes. Studio lists day passes at several locations for $50 (before taxes). At that rate, using all four complimentary passes could save you at least $200 per month. Of course, that comparison only matters if you would otherwise pay for a workspace. But even occasional users could find the passes useful — for example, when they need somewhere to work between hotel checkout and an evening flight. Unlimited Clubhouse access could be particularly useful if you live or regularly work near a participating location. Separately, eligible card accounts can receive up to $500 in statement credits each calendar year toward event space bookings at ZO or Studio locations or the purchase of a Dining Club membership (when paying with an eligible card). Event spaces start at $1,500 per hour, so the credit's value depends on whether you would otherwise book those spaces. ZO does not publish a flat, standalone retail price for a Dining Club membership, and it isn't a general restaurant credit, so don't count on using it to cover lunch during your visits. How can eligible Amex cardmembers access the spaces? Enrollment with American Express isn't required, but you'll need to activate your ZO membership online or through the ZO app (iOS; Android) before visiting. From Oct. 22, the dedicated cardmember website and app should show participating spaces and guidance on using the statement credit. You must reserve Studio visits in advance online or through the app. For eligible Amex Business Platinum and Corporate Platinum cardmembers who regularly need a place to work in one of the participating cities, complimentary ZO access could be a useful addition. If you're considering the Business Platinum, access could also help justify the card's annual fee — especially if you already pay for coworking in one of the participating cities.

item.title: Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and youâll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the panâs juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture thatâs somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great tooâjust make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish. Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Preheat oven to 425Â°. Season 6â8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1Â½â2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or Â½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Step 2Whisk together Â¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and Â¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat. Step 3Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165Â°, 25â30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate. Step 4Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12â15 minutes. Step 5Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, Â¼ cup fresh lime juice, Â½ tsp. sugar, Â¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining Â¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl. Step 6Combine Â½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed. Step 7Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

item.title: Delta’s free Wi-Fi rollout reaches 95% of planes as rivals bet big on Starlink
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Delta’s free Wi-Fi rollout reaches 95% of planes as rivals bet big on Starlink Delta Air Lines now has Wi-Fi service available throughout nearly every flight — including its longest service to Asia, Australia and the South Pacific. The Atlanta-based carrier on Tuesday announced it had closed its "last coverage gap" over the Pacific Ocean, thanks to a new satellite that just came online in the last week. Delta also said it had equipped more than 95% of its planes with the tech to support free Wi-Fi for every customer — a rollout that's expected to wrap up in the next few months. In a lot of ways, it's a milestone that's years in the making. Back in early 2023, Delta kickstarted an industry trend when it announced plans to make Wi-Fi service free to all members of its loyalty program. Yet, despite upgrading Wi-Fi tech across its fleet — and outfitting nearly 1,300 planes with the complimentary service — Delta's on-board internet has drawn plenty of scrutiny, of late. Over the past few weeks, headlines have swirled about Delta's decision not to upgrade its fleet with Starlink service, which today is generally viewed as the fastest Wi-Fi in the sky. All of Delta's biggest competitors have either begun moving over to Starlink — or plan to. That includes top rival United Airlines, which has talked up its Wi-Fi in a pointed status match offer meant to tempt longtime Delta flyers to switch their loyalties. It's probably not the backdrop Delta envisioned in January 2020, when it first laid out its vision of free web-browsing for all. But the carrier insists it's not falling behind in the increasingly competitive race by airlines to win customers with the promise of home-like internet at 35,000 feet. "Global full coverage at scale — whether you're on a regional jet or an [Airbus] A350 going to Sydney or Melbourne or Auckland — and having that on almost 1,300 airplanes? That is something that is very unique in today's world," Ranjan Goswami, Delta's chief marketing and product officer, told TPG. "That's a milestone we have," Goswami added, "that will take others some time to get there." Delta: Existing Wi-Fi getting major boost Delta also argues its existing Wi-Fi is getting faster. The carrier is in the process of moving planes over to Wi-Fi service powered by a new satellite from its top provider, Viasat, which is expected to significantly boost on-board bandwidth — and reduce slowdowns reported by customers earlier this year. That switchover — which so far has drawn "very positive" reviews, Delta says — is expected to be complete on North and South America flights by Thanksgiving. Delta is also wrapping up Wi-Fi upgrades on its fleet of regional jets and smaller Boeing 717s. Together, Goswami says, these changes should offer a noticeably better experience for passengers in the near future. "You're going to see a demonstrable improvement on overall bandwidth to the airplane," he said. "Those are improvements literally happening right now." Amazon Leo coming ... instead of Starlink Beyond that, Delta also has long-term plans to upgrade its Wi-Fi tech further. Earlier this year, the carrier became the largest in the world to sign on to new service from Amazon, which is designed to offer a web-surfing experience similar to what Starlink users find today. The downside? It's still unproven. The other? It won't begin appearing on Delta planes until 2028. In the meantime, United has already installed Starlink on 43% of its jets, according to a real-time tracker the carrier published last week — itself a sign of how competitive the airline industry's "Wi-Fi race" has gotten. Alaska Airlines is also about 40% of the way complete with Starlink installations. And Southwest Airlines last week said it expects to have its whole fleet outfitted with the tech before either of those two carriers. Each of those airlines plans to offer the service free to members of their loyalty programs, matching the policy Delta once made the industry standard — but with connectivity that will arguably be better than what Delta has today. 'Repainting the Golden Gate Bridge' Goswami, for his part, says he's "not worried," pointing to Delta's global coverage that virtually guarantees connectivity whether you're flying from Los Angeles to Sydney— or from Atlanta to Dayton. Of course, United soon will be able to offer the same breadth of connectivity. American, too. Still, Goswami expressed confidence — not only in Delta's future plans with Amazon — but also in the Wi-Fi network the airline has nearly finished installing. "It's like repainting the Golden Gate Bridge," he said. "When you finish repainting, you start painting again because you have to start over. But the beauty here is, this is based off of a really solid foundation." Related reading:

item.title: Beater Cars, Beer Bellies, and Trash By the Ton. Welcome to Gambler 500.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
A whining growl interrupted my sleep just after 6 A.M. The day’s first emissary—a minibike—darted past, launched from the apocalyptic armada surrounding me. Another dawn for the captains, oft bearded and bellied like Toby Keith in a Frankenstein fever dream, reawakening their doomed creations with WD-40 and a Craftsman wrench. They are Gamblers with a capital G, living by their own car-centric lexicon and a meager rule set. Mainly: Don’t be a dick. They are gearheads, sharp-witted jokers, iconoclasts who fix broken things—usually internal combustion engines. On this late June weekend in central Oregon’s high desert, they have congregated, 4,000 strong, as part of a sweeping movement to clean up trash-filled public lands. The weekend Gambler 500 event, also known as the OG 500 or simply Gamblertown, started small in Oregon just over a decade ago. It’s grown into a massive gathering that’s equal parts Burning Man and Baja 1000. Participants modify vehicles of every sort—cars, trucks, vans, and even school buses—into all-terrain adventure machines. Some dress in outlandish costumes. They venture into the backcountry to collect trash, have fun, and experience Mother Nature. Now there are Gambler chapters in every state, blending off-road rambling with environmental stewardship. Invariably these Gambler events draw allusions to the “Mad Max” movie franchise. The oddest of vehicles—call them hoopties, beaters, or worse—sprout appendages like gnomes or spiders or even propane-powered flamethrowers, and it’s comforting to categorize them via a cultural reference point. The only problem is that the “Mad Max” films are packed with insane characters trying to kill one another. Gamblers, while prone to some crazy moments, are battling litter as the enemy, bearing banners for Sons of Smokey, the Gambler 500’s nonprofit wildlands cleanup arm. An app (available to anyone) allows users to mark public-land dump sites, and drivers follow waypoints to remove anything from scattered trash to abandoned boats and recreational vehicles. No comprehensive report describes the extent or the costs of the trashing of U.S. public lands, though studies hint at the continuing problem. The federal Bureau of Land Management oversees about 245 million acres, primarily in 12 western states; there are millions more acres in state and federal parks and forests. In addition to Gambler-led efforts, agency and volunteer cleanups routinely encounter illegal dump sites—the work of homeless encampments, individuals evading disposal fees, and others. I had pulled into Gamblertown, in Madras, Oregon, the day before my morning minibike wake-up. Surveying a 60-acre field of mowed and yellowing grain stalks, I noted early arrivals: a desert-tan van budding a trophy buck from its roof and a giant faux cigarette from the grill, another van emblazoned with Pac-Man characters, and a bizarre menagerie of primer-colored cars displaying stickers and spraypainted slogans like defiant tattoos. My plain black 2020 Honda Pilot seemed forlornly out of place—abnormally normal. A sound I would come to know all too well greeted me: a buzzing minibike, veering around a corner. Its bearded rider wore a colonial patriot’s breeches, a frock coat and tricorn hat. His shouts outdueled the minibike’s whine. “The shitboxes are coming,” he proclaimed, mimicking Paul Revere. “The shitboxes are coming.” The Gambler 500 was born in an Oregon bar in 2014 as a cross between a question and a joke: Just how far could a beater car—one costing $500 or less— make it off-road? “In the beginning it was just me and a buddy saying, “Hey, it will be fun driving some cars around until they die,” said founder Tate Morgan. About a dozen members of a loose-knit club calling themselves the Gamblers kept the annual tradition going, adopting their own slang like “ABG” (always be gambling) and “pavement is lava”— a reference to staying off-road as much as possible. Their rallies followed preset waypoints; they departed in staggered starts from a suburban Portland saloon’s parking lot. I met Morgan in the same saloon two and a half months before this year’s event. He’s huge—6 foot 4, 240 pounds—with glacier blue eyes, unruly graying hair and a salt-and-pepper beard. A black bead of motor oil ringed his fingernails. His no-bullshit conversation style is layered with equal parts f-bombs and words like “prescient,” “ubiquitous” and “propensity.” In a measured voice, he described facing two collisions a decade ago that scarred him and raised questions over survival— his own and his newfound hobby’s. The first was discovering he had testicular cancer. The second resulted from a viral video about the 2016 Gambler 500 event. The following year, Morgan expected anywhere from a few dozen attendees to a couple of hundred. Instead, 3,000 people showed up in central Oregon. Chaos ensued. Lines. Parking headaches. U.S. Forest Service officers issued tickets for permit violations, and a citation to someone who had abandoned a broken-down vehicle. “We’re here to pick up some trash and do dumb shit.” All of which left Morgan with a decision: Kill his creation or breathe new life into it. He had grown up in Eugene, Oregon, as a true-believer environmentalist, weaned on activist/author Edward Abbey and his 1975 novel “The Monkey Wrench Gang.” Abbey encouraged others to defend the Earth through “any and every method which may be necessary.” But Morgan sought to build bridges, not detonate them. If Gamblers wanted to continue experiencing cheap outdoor fun, he decided, they needed to give something in return. Gathered around their Madras camp, Brett Hrouda, the minibike-riding man under the three-cornered hat, and his friends described their converging paths, how an ancient Subaru earned its nickname, and their succinct plans for this year’s Gambler 500. “We’re here to pick up some trash and do dumb shit,” Hrouda, 47, said. He lives near Roseburg, Oregon, and splits time as a maintenance director and invoicing manager. Shenanigans, in his friend Tom Parker’s words. Which is why Parker and his wife, Liz, left the kids at home for the big annual event. Lots of vehicles, dust, and alcohol—especially after dark. They’ve been attending Gambler events for a few years now, including smaller weekend gatherings. Hrouda tells us he finds peace while driving in the backcountry, “just following dirt roads wherever they go.” Until the trail leads to trash piles, where his patience peters out. The Gambler 500 rings on Tom Parker’s fingers spell out their disdain for litterbugs, with ominous mottos like “Throw trash, catch hands,” and more pointedly, “Kill all litterbugs.” To be clear, the organization embraces solutions and education—not violence. An event flyer, for example, emphasized “do not engage with or collect trash from active houseless population.” Liz Parker can see that her children are learning lessons from the adults. “What I love about this is that our kids are in the habit now of saying, ‘Mom, there’s trash in that ditch,’” she said. “They see it and call it out. We’re passing stewardship on to the next generation.” Tom Parker, 40, a power-line arborist from Camas Valley, Oregon, paid $350 for his first Gambler car, a Subaru, and pushed it hard for three years. Returning from a beer run, he heard sputtering. The rear-view mirror revealed clouds of black and gray smoke, signifying the Subaru’s impending death. He traded an old dirt bike for another Subaru—a 1985 GL hatchback chopped down into a makeshift pickup. The car bore no nickname until last year’s Gambler 500, when the Parkers and Hrouda strapped an abandoned sofa and other junk onto the Subaru’s back. Returning to camp, they watched in horror as an animal scurried from the sofa into the cab. It was a rat. Tom Parker braked hard, skidding. He tried to corner the rat. Liz Parker screamed and struggled to unbuckle, panicked. She wanted out. “I don’t do rodents,” she said. “There’s nothing worse than trying to bail out of a vehicle and the seatbelt won’t disengage.” The intruder didn’t survive the experience but is memorialized in the vehicle’s nickname: the Subarat. An insistent wind whipped dust and toppled the Parkers’ tent. As they righted it, a neighbor appeared, duct tape in hand. Did they have a quarter-inch adapter for a three-eighths drive torque wrench? No. I asked why it was needed. “We have too many pieces of shit,” he said. Keeping a collection of misfit motorized contraptions running can be a full-time endeavor, explained my new friend, Matt Vanella. Vanella and his crew had a rickshaw concocted from a scooter, wood and spare parts; a riding lawn mower towing a rickety wooden cart; a trike melded from bicycle and all-terrain vehicle parts, secured by scrap wood and yards of wrapped twine; and a “reverse trike,” consisting of a scooter crossbred with an ATV, supporting a forward-facing rider on a boat seat. While maintaining this Frankenstein fleet, Vanella said, he and his pals were simultaneously scouting marked dump sites through the Sons of Smokey app. They sought trophy trash to parade into camp. Something big, but not too heavy. Like a fiberglass boat. It turned out that Vanella and friends—Noah Hilton, John Rushing, Matt Wong and Eric Swanson, all from Oregon—were my camp neighbors. Swanson, 48, a cybersecurity engineer, was the mechanical mastermind. “When I was in high school, I basically lived in the auto shop,” Swanson told me. “This recruiter came to school, and he asked me, ‘Do you want to be doing this when you’re 50?’ And the answer was no, not as a full-time job. But as a hobby I need that creative outlet that’s tangible, physical.” Afterwards, Vanella, 42, a facility manager from Albany, Oregon, cajoled me into a ride on the reverse trike. He piloted it from atop the scooter, and I clambered into the front-mounted seat. No helmets for us. Just Vanella urging me to lean left, lean right to keep us from tipping. Shorts riffling in the wind, I felt giddy, thoughts ricocheting between staying upright and wondering how I would explain a concussion or broken collarbone to my wife. Making new friends. Laughing uncontrollably at high speed. Doing dumb shit. Was I hitchhiking my way onto the Gambler highway? Judge for yourself: my neighbors recorded the weekend on video. I found myself in the back seat of their Ford pickup an hour later, bouncing toward a marked trash site seven miles east of camp. Matt Wong, reading from the Sons of Smokey app, called out the turns, while Matt Vanella and the others kept a running commentary. We towed a tilting flatbed trailer. The rough gravel backroads did their best to rock me between the two Matts. You’re in a Matt sandwich, one of the front-seat wags announced. A Matt-wich, said another. That kind of imagery just writes itself, one suggested faux-helpfully, then asked: Can you actually smuggle all this into your article? (I think I just did.) The app had marked our target as “the back half of a truck.” Instead, we found the rusted remains of a semi truck’s front end, including the motor, embedded in the roadside dirt. We figured it weighed almost a ton—far too heavy to lift by hand. Lacking a winch, Hilton and friends rigged a series of heavy-duty ratchet straps and chains to the metal mass. Inch by inch, they coaxed it up the tilted flatbed. On the ride back, I recalled an old trucker anthem called “Looking at the World Through a Windshield,” and its driver “seeing everything in a little bit different light.” Well, long strips of rubber that you see Were burnt off of this rig by the likes of me And they’ll rot along the highways in this land. This big-rig remnant, having rusted on public land for years, rolled into camp on our trailer. An excavator’s jaws clamped tight and tossed it to the ground. Next stop: a metal recycler. From 2017 on, Morgan worked to establish Gambler chapters across the country. He refused to turn it into a money machine, but sought sponsors to defray costs for the annual event. Morgan established the Gambler’s non-profit arm, Sons of Smokey, with a mission of facilitating “the collection and disposal of trash from public lands, while fostering a non-partisan movement for stewardship of the outdoors.” He is proud of what they have been able to do over time—especially collecting more than 6 million pounds of trash. Rambling around and outside Morgan’s shop in West Linn, Oregon, he described the lineage of his odd collection of Gambler cars, from doorless SUVs to an ugly Saturn and a dilapidated Datsun pickup. The Gambler event no longer requires participants to invest $500 or less in their cars, but Morgan still embraces the ethic of making something out of next to nothing. That came through as he described applying layers of resin and paint on a car he was given for free. “It’s like celebrating the shittiness of it,” he said, “because you can never lose if you’re kind of shitty on purpose. Which is kind of the gambler mantra—you know we’re not playing that game of trying to outspend or be faster or bigger or stronger than someone else.” By keeping event fees low and allowing chapters in other states to use the Gambler name for free, Morgan says, “I got to keep my people.” “Then by making it about trash and conservation stewardship, I’m also betting that everyone who comes out isn’t blinded by politics or some kind of fucking asshole,” he says. “We might disagree on a lot of stuff, but if you keep that and maybe your hate speech to yourself, it’ll be fine.” As the morning buzz of minibikes mounted, my nose led me to the neighbors’ camp, where eggs, link sausages and hash browns sizzled. No trash cleanups planned today, they told me—too many maimed machines to repair. The reverse trike’s carburetor kept flooding, and the riding lawnmower’s belt was toast. Which left me hitching a new trash-hunting ride. I spied a convoy of cars and pickups forming, and an empty seat in a Toyota. The driver motioned for me to hop in. Like many of the Gamblers I met, the driver, Tyler Knudson of Corvallis, Oregon, is a military veteran. After four years as a Navy helicopter mechanic, Knudson faced no insurmountable obstacles in transplanting a Volkswagen diesel engine into his 1990 Toyota 4Runner. In arcane detail, like play-by-play for a sport I will never comprehend, Knudson recited descriptions of TDIs and ALH engine codes, adapter plates and transversely mounted motors, drive shafts and mounting points. “To keep my mental peace, I’ve resolved that I don’t care how it got here. I only care where it ends up.” After a few minutes’ drive and a bumpy turn down a dirt trail, we descended into Willow Creek Canyon. A striking tan-green horizon melded into gray clouds. Until we stopped the cars and could fully comprehend all that waited in the sagebrush. Up close, it appeared as if a garbage barge had run aground in a storm. Rusting cans. Broken bottles. Mattress springs. A rotting steer carcass. Moldy clothing. A car fender. One of our convoy members, Colton Baker of Cheney, Washington, tried fitting the scene into words. “I don’t get how people look at this beautiful view and go, ‘You know, what would be even better? Garbage,’” he said. Knudson loaned me a pair of gloves, and we all bent knees and began filling garbage bags. Knudson strapped hunks of metal and wood on the Toyota’s roof. Our convoy’s informal leader, Bob Keeton of Port Orchard, Washington, corralled us back toward camp after an hour or so, acknowledging that we had made a dent. But there might be days of trash remaining. “This whole litter issue is so complex,” he told me. “Some of it is a product of laziness. Some is desperation. To keep my mental peace, I’ve resolved that I don’t care how it got here. I only care where it ends up.” He likes hunting tires, he said. That afternoon I found him in camp by the dumpsters, his 2003 Subaru Baja piled high with discarded rubber. “I think it cost me a drive shaft, though,” he said, nodding at the Subaru. “That’s why I brought a trailer—we’re not driving it home.” Attendees keep camp neat by packing out their own trash or placing it in the dumpsters. Cars that are disabled are towed out, given away or taken to auto recyclers. “We wait to find a good deal on one that needs a motor—something that’s been used and abused and broken, then we bring it back to life. Yeah, then usually break it. Then re-break it.” Keeton’s was not the only vehicle that failed to survive the weekend. In camp, a hand-lettered cardboard sign on a green 2002 Saab 9-3 summarized the damage done by trail rocks: “Free: Hole in oil pan.” Its owner, John McKenzie of Fort Collins, Colorado, had paid $700 for the car the day before in Madras. It returned from a Saturday trail exploration on a trailer. McKenzie’s friend, Russell Caldwell of Mountain Home, Idaho, said that’s pretty much the standard Gambler auto experience. “We wait to find a good deal on one that needs a motor—something that’s been used and abused and broken, then we bring it back to life,” Caldwell said. “Yeah, then usually break it. Then re-break it.” Re-creation and recreation. Not unlike Mary Shelley’s descriptions of Dr. Frankenstein’s “whirlwind passions.” When the pressure became too great, the fictional doctor described “bending my steps towards the near Alpine valleys, (seeking) in the magnificence, the eternity of such scenes, to forget myself…” By the end of the Madras event, the 4,000 in attendance put up some substantial numbers: More than 391,000 pounds of trash collected. Fourteen cars, eight RVs, four boats. More than 2,500 tires. The organization’s cleanup efforts have won praise from land managers and outdoors enthusiasts. Environmental groups, however, contend that off-roaders—like mining operations and oil drillers—are exploiting public lands. “It’s easier to villainize the entire off-road culture than have a nuanced understanding of how other people interact with the outdoors.” Jeff Miller, senior conservation advocate for the non-profit Center for Biological Diversity, recites a litany of off-roads degradation, from wildlife habitat to archeological sites to entire ecosystems. “It’s great that someone is picking up trash, but that doesn’t offset all the environmental damage,” he said. “Off-road driving is a destructive hobby, and I don’t think it has any place on our public lands. That whole road system is the reason trash is there—it’s providing public access.” Morgan, the Gamblers’ founder, acknowledged that some off-roaders’ actions have given others a bad name. But he says the group’s cleanup results tell a clear story. “I can’t see any work being done that is more significant and visibly helpful for public lands than what we’ve accomplished,” he said. “I believe that public lands exist to serve all users. But it’s easier to villainize the entire off-road culture than have a nuanced understanding of how other people interact with the outdoors.” Word of mouth, amplified by the Gamblers’ robust social media presence, continues to reverberate. In July, a friends group of Utah’s Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument approached Morgan about partnering on cleanup efforts. “I see trash all over southern Utah, into Arizona and as far south as the Grand Canyon,” said Jackie Grant, executive director of Grand Staircase Escalante Partners. “We occasionally will see something huge—a camper or vehicle—that we don’t have the capacity for. I’m hoping we can come together and make a really big impact on trash.” Similarly, BLM land managers in Idaho report a “vast landscape that has just been trashed,” with inadequate staff to address the issue. National and Oregon BLM spokespersons said volunteer efforts, including by the Gambler group, are both welcome and “inspiring.” Scientists tell us that our brains automatically assign individuals into social categories so we can understand their motivations and better predict their actions. But when we met before the event, Morgan had warned against overgeneralizing. “These are the nicest, kindest people you will ever meet,” he told me. “If you need gas, if you need help fixing your car, if you need a ride to the hospital—these people are there for you.” This I know to be true. Because a couple of years back, as I knelt beside my Dodge pickup’s flat tire on a roadside, a stranger stopped to help. I asked him about the Gambler stickers on his rear window, and his answers—crazy car fun mixed with cleaning up public lands—ultimately led me to invite myself along for this weekend adventure. Where I met mostly white men, one of whom offered me a beer and happily explained fitting a fiberglass boat on top of a Buick, dubbing the creation the “Lamboatghini.” I met a woman, 8 months pregnant, behind the wheel of a one-ton Ford pickup towing a flatbed trailer piled high with recovered junk. And met John Thompson of Burbank, Washington, a longtime Gambler, whose battered, tie-dyed 1993 Oldsmobile Cutlass Ciera has survived 222,000 miles and has been submerged in a pond. Thompson paid $200 for it in 2018, when it was vanilla white and bore some resemblance to a normal vehicle. “If my 18-year-old self saw me driving this thing now he’d kick my ass,” Thompson said. “But this car will probably outlive me.” Thompson nicknamed it “Lazarus.” Seemed like nearly every Gambler was determined to pen a new chapter on rising from the dead. As I prepared to leave camp, I found my neighbors huddled with funereal solemnity, clutching beer cans instead of flowers. Their eyes examined the remains. Behind the riding lawnmower, the crude wooden cart sprawled on its side. Splintered frame boards told a tale: A hard right turn, and Newton’s first law of motion sent the cart—and its occupants, Vanella and Rushing—tumbling. Neither was seriously injured, though Vanella displayed a skinned knee like a war wound. “I’m kind of happy because now maybe we can throw this cart away,” he said. But his friends weren’t in mourning – they were plotting. A couple of tie-down straps might reunite the cart and its frame, at least temporarily. “We’ll get ‘er fixed in no time,” Hilton said. I wished them well and proffered a round of handshakes. Wheeling the dusty Pilot out of camp, I turned northwest onto U.S. Route 26, passing a station wagon bearing a discarded sofa on its roof. One more load arriving. After two days of ABG (always be gambling), I held a new appreciation for what lies hidden beyond the asphalt in the high desert’s sagebrush and juniper. I’d seen the weird and the wonderful, witnessed maimed machinery being nursed back to life, donned gloves and filled trash bags, and found hope lurking under a veneer of garbage and indifference. The snow-topped Cascades and a twisting roadway loomed between me and home, affording a couple of hours to ponder cycles of ruin and renewal, loss and resurrection. Pavement is lava, and I had 93 miles to burn. Four-time Lowell Thomas Award-winner Alex Pulaski is a former travel editor turned freelance writer. His travel articles have appeared in Afar, National Geographic, The Boston Globe, The Los Angeles Times, The Washington Post, and other publications.

item.title: Easy Homemade Cranberry Sauce
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
This easy cranberry sauce recipe has been a fixture on my familyâs Thanksgiving table for years, served alongside my motherâs elaborate Indian-inspired holiday dishes. With just 10 minutes on the stove and a handful of ingredientsâfresh or frozen cranberries, sugar, orange zest, and waterâit delivers the bright, tangy flavor that cuts through all the richness of the holiday meal. My mom started making cranberry sauce after tasting a homemade version at a friendâs house. Over time, she made it her own, dialing back the sugar for extra tang and adding orange zest for brightness. Weâve tried fancier versions with maple syrup, chiles, and warm spices, but always come back to this stripped-down sauce. Anything more dulls the sharp cranberry bite we love. A splash of orange liqueur is entirely optional, and you can swap some or all of the white sugar for light brown sugar. Best of all, you can make the sauce up to five days ahead, leaving one less thing to think about on Thanksgiving Day. Can I use frozen cranberries to make cranberry sauce? Absolutely. Fresh and frozen cranberries both work, and there's no need to thaw frozen berries before cooking. They may take a little longer to burst and become jammy. Can I leave out the orange liqueur? Yes. The liqueur adds another layer of citrus flavor, but it's entirely optional. Brandy-based Grand Marnier brings warm, vanilla-like notes, while Cointreau offers a cleaner, brighter orange flavor. You can also simply leave it out; the orange zest provides fruity brightness on its own. Why is my cranberry sauce runny? Cranberries contain natural pectin, which helps the sauce thicken as it cools. If yours still seems thin once cooled, return it to a simmer and cook until it coats the back of a spoon and holds a line when you run your finger through it. What can I do with leftover cranberry sauce? Leftover cranberry sauce is practically a Thanksgiving bonus. Spread it on turkey sliders or buttered toast, spoon it over a baked sweet potato, make jammy swirl cookies, or blend a dollop into a milkshake. Need to make a substitution? - Cook 1 (12-oz.) bag fresh or frozen cranberries, Â¾ cup granulated sugar, 1â2 Tbsp. Grand Marnier, Cointreau, or other orange liqueur (if using), 1 Tbsp. finely grated orange zest, a pinch of kosher salt, and 1 cup water in a medium saucepan over medium heat, stirring often to prevent scorching, until cranberries burst and sauce becomes jammy and coats a spoon, about 10 minutes.Let cool before serving. Do ahead: Cranberry sauce can be made 5 days ahead. Transfer to an airtight container; cover and refrigerate until well chilled. item.title: I closed my eyes and stuck my finger on a map of western Europe: ‘This is where we’re going on holiday!’
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
An unruly rabble bursts on to the street: a noisy eruption, bubbling towards us. This isnât closing time on the Croisette in Cannes. A flock of sheep bustles past our cottage towards the shade of a huge chestnut tree, driven by three generations of herders and their dogs. The waterlike cacophony of their bells slows until only the odd tink tink punctuates the cicadasâ hum. The sheep graze, the shepherds doze off, and the mountain hamlet is still again. My partner and I had set off by Eurostar less than 24 hours before, yet this place felt a world away from the ad agency where I work. Weâd booked cheap tickets to Paris months ago, intending to plan a trip on from there by train. As our departure approached, Instagram seemed to be full of aspirational, yet similar, holiday photos, and almost every other TikTok post I flicked past offered the promise of a hidden destination â¦ discovered. I find ratings, reviews and recommendations just as reassuring as the next person, especially when faced with a limited holiday allowance. The safety of the search bar helps to give me the confidence that Iâm spending my hard earned money as wisely as possible. I work in a world that runs on data and optimisation and I love it, but I wondered whether Iâd optimised the adventure out of my own holidays. So, we tried a simple experiment. We closed down the tabs and opened a map of western Europe. Embracing a bit of low-tech randomness, we chose to let chance decide our trip. I shut my eyes and we promised to go wherever my finger landed. I waved my hand like a magic wand and pointed, then took a deep breath, eyes still closed. What if we ended up in some industrial wasteland? But we were in luck. My finger landed upon the commune of Saint-Hilaire-de-Lavit in CÃ©vennes, a place weâd never heard of and almost certainly would never have found by searching âplaces to go in Franceâ. After overnighting in Paris, a three-hour fast train zipped us down to Montpellier, where we hired a car. We stopped for provisions in a Lidl on the edge of town, stocking up for the whole trip â we werenât expecting to find any shops at our journeyâs end. A short drive inland, and the roads began to get narrower and more sparsely populated. As they climbed and zigzagged into this south-east corner of the Massif Central, we entered a south of France far removed from the honeypots served up by algorithms. We pulled into a grassy layby on a high mountain pass where there was one other car parked. Had we arrived? Weâd followed the cottage ownerâs directions as there was no signal here for Google Maps, so it was hard to tell. Stretching our legs in the fresh, cool air, the first thing we noticed was the quiet. No traffic, no tourists. Just stillness. But the languid buzz of big insects flying by and the whirring chorus of cicadas told us this place was alive. Squinting into the low sun, we saw someone waving. Our host, Guilaine, had appeared as if by magic and was beckoning us to the cottage a little farther down the road. We had found the hamlet of Les Ayres: a cluster of maybe 10 stone buildings, 800 metres above sea level. The rough-walled dwellings huddled either side of the narrow road, making the most of the tiny strand of level ground before the mountainâs spine fell away into steep forest. A long wooden awning and some outdoor tables suggested a cafe opposite our cottage, but the building was shuttered, and Les Ayresâ only potential customers seemed to be ourselves and Guilaine. She took us to the back of our accommodation, to a veranda that looked out over chestnut and pine-clad mountains rolling into the horizon. Itâs a landscape that appears wild but has actually been shaped by farming, forestry and the seasonal movement of livestock for thousands of years. The next morning, as I watched the sheep and their guardians settle down in the shade, I felt the ancientness of the place. Shepherds must have moved their flocks along the same path and most likely slept under the same chestnut trees for centuries. Traditional farming practices endure here in part because the area is veined with crystal-clear mountain streams, meaning animals traversing the paths are never too far from a drink. So rather than opening the internet, we let these ancient tracks, known as drailles, guide our hikes. We took sweaty, daylong expeditions without seeing another human or hearing the sound of cars. The forests protected us from the worst of the sunâs blaze but, on our first trek, the real treat came when we rounded a corner to find that what we thought was the sound of wind in the pines was actually water gushing through a narrow gorge below us. Another couple of switchbacks and we arrived at a deep, clear pool created as the stream carved a corner into the rock. Dappled sunlight filtered down through trees clinging to the steep-sided valley, creating spotlights for damselflies to dart through. We stopped for a picnic and a swim in the freezing mountain water, picking wild strawberries from the bank for dessert. We discovered that these shady, secluded river pools were waiting for us on all the paths that led down from our cottage. As well as being the ultimate pit stops for mid-hike refreshment, they were teeming with wildlife â tadpoles wriggled in the shallows, fish flickered in the depths and a huge variety of butterflies, dragonflies and other insects skimmed the surface. We even saw a snake swimming across water weâd been submerged in just minutes before. We spent our last afternoon reading on a rock, summoning the energy to walk back up the mountain (one drawback of staying high up on a pass). We watched the sun swing over the water and the light change as the day wore on. When the air began to cool, we worked our way back towards the cottage. As the path turned into an empty, single-track road, a car approached â a big event after so much seclusion. It was Guilaine â the only person apart from the shepherds weâd encountered. In the evening, as the light faded, the sound of brass band practice drifted towards our veranda. Later, owls called to each other and a distant wild boar screeched into the quiet night. None of this had appeared in my search results. There was no review promising unexpected trumpeting, no listicle recommending the best pool for swimming among tadpoles, and no algorithm that could have told me where the sheep would pass on that first morning. We hadnât looked at our phones for days â maybe that was the real discovery.

item.title: America’s Newest National Park, Chiricahua, Is a Wonderland. I Spent My Honeymoon Hiking There.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Sunset along the Echo Canyon hiking trail among hoodoos and rock pillars at Chiricahua National Monument near Wilcox Arizona. (Photo: Getty) What to know: Chiricahua is the first U.S. national park in six years. The bill to redesignate Chiricahua National Monument as America’s 64th national park was passed by the Senate on September 30, 2026, and signed by President Trump on October 20. Our writer shares what it’s like to visit Chiricahua, hiking its winding trails alongside towering rock pinnacles and incredible biodiversity. Chiricahua, located 120 miles east of Tucson, is now the state’s fourth national park, joining Grand Canyon, Petrified Forest, and nearby Saguaro. Chiricahua is pronounced cheer-uh-KAH-wuh (or cheery-cow-ah). The trail we are hiking isn’t strenuous, but my husband and I, committed-relationship status as fresh as the snow under our feet, are struggling for words. Rock stacks rise above our heads, and hundreds of pinnacles dot the landscape beyond. Boulders splashed with lime green and black lichen perch nonchalantly atop each other, and canyons wind around rusty outcrops. Being in the middle of Chiricahua National Monument feels like being dwarfed by a sea of massive navigation cairns and those knobby towers of dribbled sand children make at the beach. The Apache name for this place translates to “Land of Standing-Up Rocks.” It’s a succinct, accurate description compared to what our pens scribble in the first pages of our joint adventure journal. Exploring Chiricahua National Monument will become a core experience on our honeymoon trip and, standing in the forest of stone searching for ways to voice our amazement, we know it. Memories of that mesmerizing hike, which we did this past February, rushed back into our minds today. On October 20, 2026, 102 years after it was first named a national monument, Chiricahua became the first U.S. national park in six years. The bill to redesignate Chiricahua National Monument, located 120 miles east of Tucson, as a national park was passed by the Senate on September 30, 2026, and signed by President Trump on October 20, 2026. To those with personal, historical, and scientific ties to Chiricahua, this is a big moment. A monument is designated by a president—in Chiricahua’s case Calvin Coolidge— via the Antiquities Act of 1906, often to protect a singular specific resource. To be eligible for national park status, a place usually boasts a vast chunk of scarce resources or a particularly scenic landscape worth protecting. From the ground on the Echo Canyon trail, one of several trails of varying difficulty that weave through boulder spires, the natural and recreational value of Chiricahua is obvious. Despite other areas of significant natural and historical beauty also in the race to become America’s 64th national park, Chiricahua is special, and not only to us. The monument contains rich history, including ties to the Chiricahua Apache people. Archaeologists are still discovering who once walked through this landscape and how it was used. The geological surprises around every corner are the most noticeable draw, but hiking through the unique blended landscapes and environments gives an intimate view of the incredible exhibition of biodiversity it supports. During our late February visit to Arizona, the southeastern corner of the state is blanketed under a fresh snowfall, so we have the trails to ourselves. The cool shoulder seasons are the best times to stroll through the park: spring for wildflower season and fall for the quieter trails and more availability at the park’s only place to stay, Bonita Canyon Campground. The campground facilities may be limited to water, flush toilets and garbage bins, but its beautiful shady pine and oak setting is just a taste of the stunning landscapes awaiting up the road. Chiricahua National Park blends four distinct ecoregions—two deserts (Sonoran and Chiricahuan) and two highland regions (Rocky Mountains and Sierra Madre)—into a unique mix of flora and fauna. Here, where many Mexican bird species are at the northern end of their range, the birding is fantastic. As we hike, the habitats evolve from cacti meadows to blooming manzanita thickets to towering pine forests exuding spice as the sun gains strength. We keep one eye trained on the hoodoos, one peeled for wildlife, hoping to spot a Chiricahua fox squirrel, coatimundi, rattlesnake or javelina, but the diverse wildlife that call the park home don’t seem to be fans of the winter conditions either. Our surroundings are also evolving as we walk. One moment we have an expansive view of the hazy blue desert beyond the range, overlooking expanses of burned landscapes. A little later, we are deep in a tan canyon, twisting around weathered columns. We round a corner and Duck-on-a-rock, with its long bill perched high above the trees, is an easy landmark to identify within a sea of natural splendor. The stacked rhyolite and vast rolling landscapes of this mountain range—one of several desert isolated high altitude ranges known as Sky Islands—tell of a turbulent geological history. It’s hard to imagine violent volcanoes creating the otherworldly landscape framing the peaceful, sun dappled paths. Two rocky columns appear along the trail, leaning in for what looks like an eternal kiss. There’s no one around, so we take the inspiration for a smooch. We are on our honeymoon, after all. Our rambling route, from Mushroom Rock to the Heart of Rocks Loop, takes us past gravity-defying stacks sculpted over time by wind and water. We wonder if an ancient or historical someone once stood in this spot, also agape at the Big Balanced-Rock, a massive boulder precariously perched atop a monolith. Given the Chiricahua’s Indigenous and recorded pasts, it’s highly likely. Becoming a national park is a big deal for a well-deserving gem like Chiricahua, is now the state’s fourth, joining Grand Canyon, Petrified Forest, and nearby Saguaro. The status will benefit southeastern Arizona’s recreational economy by attracting tourists, but it’s also about preserving the unique landscape and its inhabitants. Chiricahua National Park is no stranger to protection efforts. The Civilian Conservation Corps, a result of President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s Depression-era program to both create employment and help protect and develop resources, were key in preserving the ancient pinnacles my new husband and I crane our necks at. Today, scientists continue to track water resources and actively manage invasive plant species with deceptively cute names like Malta starthistle and Lehmann lovegrass. Eventually, we tear ourselves away, mindblown. On the scenic drive out of the park, the Faraway Ranch house—once an early homestead turned dude ranch and now a historic point of interest—flashes by. The last operators of the ranch, Lillian Erickson and her husband Edward Riggs, were always convinced the grandeur of the area deserved special protection. As newlyweds, their 1923 bid to achieve national park status for the so-called Wonderland of Rocks ultimately led to a monument designation, but now, a century later, they have finally gotten their wish. Sylvia Dekker is an Alberta-based outdoor and travel writer who thinks an ideal honeymoon is spent hiking, tracking wildlife, and sleeping in a tent where there is less snow than at home in Canada. Her work, often on nature and outdoor experiences, has appeared in the Toronto Star, Explore Magazine, and Mountain Life Magazine.

The islands tend to steal the limelight when it comes to Grecian beach breaks and there’s good reason why people visit time and time again. But beyond their glittering shores is a mainland that’s home to some of the country’s most beautiful beaches, and some of its most sublime stays, too. Halkidiki, a three-pronged peninsula in the north, is just one example. On the third ‘finger’ you’ll find Mount Athos – or the Holy Mountain – a UNESCO World Heritage Site that’s home to 20 Orthodox monasteries and 2,000 monks (only men can visit). But scattered across the trident-like peninsula, you’ll also find some of the country’s most loved hotels – and notably, some exceptional options for families that, despite the cacophony of kids' chatter, can still feel like restful and restorative stays. You’ll fly into Thessaloniki, so if you have the time and inclination (and let’s face it, you’ll ideally do this without kids), then leave a night or two to explore the city – it’s the second largest in Greece and has a thriving food and bar scene thanks to the large student population. As a long-time lover of a Greek escape, this is my list of the best hotels in Halkidiki. item.title: All the Ways to Book a Private Jet—Or At Least Snag a Seat on One
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
I've often heard it said that once you've flown first class, you're ruined for any lesser form of travel. But once you've flown private, you've got a whole new lens through which to view air travel. Primarily, one in which TSA lines are nonexistent, security checks are not your problem, and rather than mill around a gate waiting for your boarding group to be called, you can saunter on up to the plane at your leisure. It's an entirely different ballgame. I learned this firsthand when I flew with FlexJet from New Jersey's Teterboro Airport to Paris this summer. It was my first time flying private, and I couldn't get over how seamless the experience was. While a commercial transatlantic flight would have left me feeling tired and ragged, my body barely registered the six-hour journey. I could get up from my plush leather seat whenever I wanted to stretch my legs, freshen up in the spacious bathroom with seemingly endless amenities (no really, options ranged from Burt's Bees lip balm to Neutrogena makeup remover wipes, tissue packets, hand sanitizers and lotionsâ¦even playing cards!), or chat with fellow passengers over a glass of Champagne. Don't even get me started on the mealsâpastries, quiche, and yogurt parfaits for breakfast; tuna niÃ§oise salads for lunchâall made fresh by our personal chef Francesco, who was the bar manager at Villa d'Este before coming to FlexJet. For the first time, I found myself wishing the flight was longer. Indulgent as it was, my trip with FlexJet also demonstrated that private jet travel no longer requires access to your own personal G5. In response to the pandemic's private jet boom, new booking options have emerged for travelers looking to take to the skies in seclusionâand many of them with ticket prices that deliver less sticker shock than you might imagine. Even though social distancing may not be the term du jour any longer, the state of commercial aviation certainly has travelers keen to fly on their own time. âPrivate aviation has experienced remarkable growth over the past several years, reflecting a fundamental shift in what travelers value most,â says Flexjet CEO Mike Silvestro. âTime has become the ultimate luxury, and people are looking for greater flexibility, efficiency, and a more personalized travel experience.â However, for those who, like myself, are a newly initiated high-flier, navigating the multitude of companies and different categories of private air travel can feel overwhelming. Below is a primer on some of the various ways to score a seat on a private aircraftâfrom fly-share services and traditional charters to fractional ownership, and more. These days, all it takes is a strong Wi-Fi connection (and a handy app or two) to get yourself onto a private plane. A number of services connect fliers directly with charter operators, allowing you to browse, book, and buy within minutes. FlyHouseâwhich acquired JetASAP in 2024 and Sun Air Jets in 2025, allowing it to expand its tech and operational capabilities as well as its geographic reachâallows fliers to secure and book private flights directly from their smartphones. It has access to more than 2,300 aircraft across the US, with a variety of midsize to ultra-long-range jets. Within the app, travelers can coordinate not just private flights but hotels, ground transportation, dining, and curated experiences too. Fliers are never required to pay a commissionâjust punch in a flight request, which includes your airport of departure and preferred flight times, and live operators will respond with quotes and can answer any questions. Private charters typically cost between $3,000 to $12,000 per in-flight hour. The FlyJetsÂ platform debuted in January 2020, and operates like a travel search engine, allowing customers to filter results via their preferred aircraft size, location, and desired departure time and book via the website or app. Prices can be as much as 50% lower than the costs of an average charter, and booking options include full charters, seats on shared charters, and group-purchases. Travelers can even bid on flights that lack a fixed price.Â They can also earn rewards for flying green, with carbon offsets delivered directly to their user dashboard. Jettly was designed to simplify the act of chartering a private plane. It has a network of more than 23,000 aircrafts, and lets user search for one-way flights, round-trip tickets, and multi-city travels, flying out of popular airports like Van Nuys in LA, Teterboro in New Jersey, and Miami International Airport. Flights can be arranged within a few hours, but the platform recommends booking several days in advance to ensure the widest aircraft availability and best pricing. While a membership is not required, Jettly does offers memberships that of course come with perksâlower hourly rates, waived booking fees, and access to things like empty leg alerts. Founded in 2010 and based in London, Victor is another digital marketplace that prides itself of transparent, real-time pricing (including the aircraft tail number and photos of the aircraft, so you know exactly what to expect) and carbon-offset initiatives. An account is required, but registering is free; once you're in, you're assigned a Personal Account Manager to handle all your travels. XO, a private jet marketplace that was acquired by Vista in 2018, has access to thousands of safety-vetted aircraft with real-time pricing. The mobile app and website offers both âbuy as you flyâ and membership options, with featured flight deals ranging from $3,000 to $90,000. If you want to reserve an entire plane for a one-time flight, private jet charters are the most straightforward way to book. Charter companies work with dozens of private air operators to book on-demand flights and manage door-to-door logistics, with no long-term commitment required. Many also offer the option to purchase a jet card, which you can load up either with a fixed number of flight hours or with money you spend like a debit card. Founded in 2013,Â Wheels UpÂ provides access to more than 1,500 aircraft, with a fleet that includes gold-standard planes like the King Air 350iÂ and Citation X. Initially a membership-only offering, the Wheels Up app launched in 2021 widened to pool so that nonmembers could browse and book one-off flights. In the years since, the brand has continued to iterate on its membership tiers, including launching a Signature Membership program in 2025, giving anyone willing to fork over $200,000 guaranteed nationwide availability and 365-days-a-year access to its fleet of Phenom 300 series and Challenger 300 series aircraft; oh, and Delta perks tooânamely, Delta SkyMiles Diamond Medallion status. One of the biggest global aircraft charter brokers in the world, ACS charters private jets (for both business and leisure), group aircrafts, and even cargo planes. Users fill out a simple form to get a quote back quickly, and then a dedicated account manager will suggest aircrafts that might suit your needsâconsidering they have access to 50,000 private airplanes and 130 different aircraft types, this is quite helpful. While costs vary, estimates provided say a 40-minute flight in a small plane could cost around $2,800, while a 1.5-hour flight in a midsize jet will be closer to $34,500. Fly-share companies are the easiest on the wallet. Companies like Surf Air and JSX enable travelers to snag a coveted seat on a private jet charterâsometimes for as little as $249 each wayâsharing space with only a handful of other passengers and enjoying perks like no security lines and departure fromÂ private terminals. Started in 2019 by Uber cofounder Garrett Camp, Aero offers white-glove service on a fleet of sleek 16-seater black jets. The company flies to private terminals in Aspen, Colorado; Los Cabos, Mexico; Los Angeles (Van Nuys); Maui; Miami; New York (Westchester and NYC); and West Palm Beach, Florida. Tickets on these semi-private flights (unless your whole crew books one together) range from around $1,000 to $3,000 per leg, and pets are welcome on board. This summer, Aero launched an exciting new seasonal route on a Gulfstream IV-SP taking passengers from from Van Nuys in LA into New York City, with a helicopter transfer via Blade out to East Hampton. The weekend flights went out on Fridays and returned on Sundays, with seats costing $7,570. BladeÂ is a popular choice for city-based travelers, with dozens and dozens of established flight routes. It connects fliers not just with jets but also turboprops, seaplanes, and helicopters in their contracted fleet via a user-friendly app. This year, its BladeOne planes are back to offering seasonal service fromÂ NYCÂ toÂ Miami and Palm Beach (on planes powered by Aero) from November 2026 through May 2027. There's no membership required and fliers can purchase multipacks of flight passes on certain routes (the New York to South Florida packs start at $2,300 per seat). A Traveler reader favorite, Tradewind Aviation operates semi-private scheduled routes and private charters in the northeast (US) and the Caribbean. Specifically, its aircraft bases are in Oxford, Connecticut; Westchester, New York; Stuart, Florida; and San Juan, Puerto Rico; though charter flights are available throughout the regions. Dog lovers may already know about Bark Air, a semi-private flight carrier designed around luxury travel for pups and their owners, with planes typically carrying around nine human guests. Read more about the airline here. JSX, a semi-private carrier, offers flights on 30-seat jets, out of private terminals, starting at $249 each way. The company currently serves 18 markets including Austin, Texas; Los Angeles; Miami; and Westchester County, New York. Thanks to a partnership with United Airlines, travelers can earn United MileagePlus miles for their flights. With fractional ownership, your piece of the pie is allocated in hours. Owners purchase a portion or share of an aircraft, which is doled out in hours of flight time. The bigger the share, the more hours you get in the air. Flextjet's fleet of more than 300 aircrafts (helicopters included) operating in the US and Europe includes Embraer'sÂ super-light Phenom 300 and the ultra-long-range Gulfstream G450, and offer room for up to 15 passengers. The brand operates nine private terminals in oft-visited destinationsâNew York and New Jersey, Florida, California, Texas, and Farnborough, Englandâwith more on the way, though travelers aren't limited to those places; Flexjet aircrafts can fly into thousands of airports around the world, including ones not served by commercial airlines. Flight time can be purchased in 50-hour increments per year, and while you're purchasing equity in a specific jet, the plane you fly in can differ based on a given trip's needs. Before you commit, members of the sales team will talk through who you fly with and where you typically go in order to determine what aircraft level and time commitment is best suited to you. Bookings can be done fairly last minute (10 hours out for domestic flights; 48 hours for international ones); costs per hour start at $7,000 for a light jet like the Phenom 300 and go up to $23,000 per hour for an ultra-long-range aircraft like a Gulfstream G700. NetJets, the granddaddy of private aviation companies, has been at it for awhileâBerkshire Hathaway acquired the company in 1998, and its fleet keeps on expanding, with 80+ new jets to be added into their fleet in 2026. Options range from light jets that fit up to 6 passengers to long-range jets with room for 14, with access to over 5,000 airports worldwide. Costs start at $215,000 for a jet card with 275 days of annual access; costs depend on chosen purchase method and aircraft type. For more frequent fliers, membership programs can be attractive. Through tiered subscription options, youâll pay a monthly or annual fee that unlocks access to an entire fleet of aircrafts that can then be booked on demand. VistaJetâs fleet of silver and red aircraft includes corporate jets and the long-range Bombardier Global 7500, which has a bedroom and full-size kitchen. Membership options include VistaJet VJ25, a three-year private flight subscription for those who fly between 25 and 49 hours per year, with the option to roll over up to 20% of your hours to the following year if you happen to fly less. Sentient Jet is the inventor of the Jet Card, which allows users to buy 25 hours of flights at a time and choose the aircraft size that fits their needs. The SJ25 Card offers access to light aircraft at a price of $183,100 for 25 hours; SJ25+ gets you 25 hours on mid, super-mid, and large-cabin jets for $235,850. This Boston-based private aviation provider also offers charters, but an easier entry point is their membership program. The Explorer Membership guarantees access to light, mid, super-mid, and heavy-cabin aircraft year-round, with no blackout dates for a surprisingly low base fareâa $16,500 initial investment, $4,500 annual dues, and pay-as-you-go rates. Explorer100 members receive fixed-rate pricing across four cabin-size categories. With an $11,500 initial investment and the same annual dues ($4,500), you'll get a 12-month rate lock.
