item.title: What will El Niño mean for travel? The ‘super’ weather event is impacting conditions globally – here's how it could affect travel plans now and in the future
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
El NiÃ±o has officially arrived, and some forecasters are suggesting it could eventually develop into a rare âsuperâ event capable of dramatically altering weather patterns across much of the planet, from the safari plains of East Africa to the coral atolls of the Indian Ocean. For travellers, that could mean everything from a quieter Atlantic hurricane season to worsening wildfire smoke in Southeast Asia, stress on reefs in the Pacific and floods, landslides and transport disruption across parts of the Americas â with the most significant impacts likely to peak in December 2026 before gradually weakening as winter goes on. Previous El NiÃ±os have brought major devastation across continents. From 2015 to the following year, severe drought affected parts of southern Africa, Ethiopia and Central America, vast fires burned through drought-stricken Indonesian forests and peatlands and exceptional ocean heat contributed to the longest global coral bleaching event then recorded. More recently, the strong El NiÃ±o recorded in 2024 helped propel that year to the highest global temperature yet measured, with extreme rainfall and flooding killing more than 180 people in southern Brazil and displacing around 600,000. In June 2026, the European Commissionâs Joint Research Centre (JRC) stated that âIn Europe, this El NiÃ±o could be strong enough to flip the pattern: instead of colder-than-normal autumn temperatures that typically accompany it, Europe may experience warmer-than-normal conditions, with that warmth building towards spring 2027â. The House of Commons Library reports that the meteorological effects of El NiÃ±o on Europe could result in more extreme winter weather in the UK in 2027. What makes people so apprehensive of El NiÃ±o is that it rarely stays where it starts. A patch of unusually warm water in the tropical Pacific can eventually influence everything from rainfall in Kenya to drought around Victoria Falls, wildfire risk in Indonesia and winter storms in California. âWe need to prepare for a potentially strong El NiÃ±o event,â World Meteorological Organisation secretary-general Celeste Saulo warned a few months ago, pointing to the prospect of worsening drought, heavy rain and heatwaves both on land and at sea. UN secretary-general AntÃ³nio Guterres was blunter, saying El NiÃ±o would âpour fuel on the fire of a warming worldâ, allowing its effects to travel farther and strike harder. The most alarming forecasts raise the possibility that the event could eventually cross into âsuper El NiÃ±oâ territory, an unofficial term generally applied when temperatures in a key part of the tropical Pacific rise at least 2Â°C above normal, with such events occurring only around once every decade or so, and historically leaving a trail of droughts, floods, fires and failed harvests across several continents. âWhen you have an El NiÃ±o over what climate change already brought, the risks are enormous,â Francisco Aquino, head of the climate centre at Brazilâs Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul, told Reuters. Piers Forster, professor of physical climate change at the University of Leeds, meanwhile described the developing event as a potential âwindow into the futureâ â a preview of weather extremes that may become increasingly ordinary as the planet continues to warm. Here's everything travellers need to know about this year's El NiÃ±o weather system. What exactly is El NiÃ±o? El NiÃ±o is a recurring warming of the central and eastern tropical Pacific that can disturb weather thousands of miles beyond the ocean where it begins. Under usual conditions, easterly trade winds push warm surface water westwards towards Indonesia and northern Australia. Cold, nutrient-rich water rises from the depths off Peru and Ecuador, while the warmer western Pacific produces some of the worldâs most dramatic tropical rainstorms. During El NiÃ±o, those trade winds weaken, and the great reservoir of warm water begins sliding back towards the east, suppressing the cold upwelling off South America and dragging the principal zone of tropical thunderstorms across the Pacific with it. That interferes with the Walker circulation â the vast loop of rising and sinking air above the tropics â and sends a series of atmospheric ripples around the planet, with results that can appear entirely disconnected from their source. Is El NiÃ±o now officially underway? According to several meteorological agencies around the world, including the World Meteorological Organisation, yes, El NiÃ±o now officially underway. El NiÃ±o conditions have been present since spring 2026 and are now "firmly established". El NiÃ±o continues to strengthen, with a strong-to-very strong El NiÃ±o likely through January-March 2027. The NOAA released their U.S. winter outlook on 15 October predicting heavy rain across much of the country. âWhile higher chances of rain and snow may bring relief to drought-afflicted areas, too much precipitation on dry soil can fuel destructive flash floods and mudslides. Now is the time for communities and individuals to plan ahead for the upcoming winter.â Australia's Bureau of Meteorology says El NiÃ±o has reached near-record levels, with further intensification expected. Their October assessment reports says that these average sea surface temperatures are now at their highest on record: +2.81Â°C. What would El NiÃ±o mean for UK weather? The question many of us in the UK are asking; will El NiÃ±o bring a stormy autumn and a colder winter to the UK? We're slightly less affected here than many tropical regions are. Though according to the UK Government's Office for Science report, we're slightly more at risk of heavy rainfall and stormy weather from October till December, with more cold snaps predicted for early 2027 which could bring snow and ice. Why is this particular El NiÃ±o attracting so much attention? Most international models currently suggest that the event will become at least moderate, with a strong event also possible. Some longer-range projections extend into the much rarer territory sometimes described as a âsuper El NiÃ±oâ. That's generally used for an exceptionally powerful event in which temperatures across an important section of the central tropical Pacific rise roughly 2Â°C or more above average â and only a small number of modern El NiÃ±os have reached comparable strength. All three became associated with severe and simultaneous weather disruption across several continents. Yet the most extreme projections for 2026 remain just that. NOAA has said there is still substantial uncertainty over peak strength, with no single category dominating its probabilities. Stronger El NiÃ±os also make certain consequences more likely rather than guaranteeing them. The amount of heat already sitting beneath the Pacific explains why forecasters are watching so closely â and the WMO has urged governments to prepare for a potentially strong event capable of worsening drought, heavy rain and heatwaves on land and at sea. When will travellers begin to notice the effects? The first visible signs for travellers may be slightly subtler â unusually dry conditions in Bali, greener-than-usual safari landscapes in East Africa, or a quieter Atlantic hurricane season than forecasters had expected. El NiÃ±o usually develops between spring and early summer, strengthens through autumn and peaks between November and February. Its effects often then continue through the following spring or summer, while slower consequences â such as depleted reservoirs, damaged reefs, altered river levels and stressed wildlife populations â may last considerably longer. During summer and autumn 2026, travellers could begin seeing the first shifts in tropical cyclone activity, Southeast Asian rainfall, wildfire conditions and the Asian and African monsoons. From around October, attention is likely to turn towards East Africaâs short rains, drought risks in southern Africa and Australia, and the possibility of heavy rain across Peru and Ecuador. The influence on the US, Canada and parts of East Asia usually becomes clearest during the northern hemisphere winter, particularly between December and March. Yet its effect on global temperature may peak later still. El NiÃ±o releases heat stored in the tropical Pacific into the atmosphere, meaning the year after an event develops can be exceptionally warm. The strong 2023-24 El NiÃ±o helped push 2024 to record global temperatures, and the return of the phenomenon has already raised concerns that 2027 could challenge those records again. What could happen to travel during the 2026â27 El NiÃ±o? The potential impacts are wide-ranging and vary dramatically by country. The same climate pattern that brings blue skies to Bali could contribute to flooding in Peru, while travellers enjoying greener safari landscapes in Kenya may be doing so during the same season that drought grips southern Africa. Across Indonesia and parts of maritime Southeast Asia, suppressed rainfall could initially look like ideal holiday weather, but as the dry season deepens, the same conditions can produce water stress, forest and peat fires, and smoke capable of spreading into Singapore and Malaysia. East Africa may face the reverse problem later in the year. Stronger October to December rains could turn safari landscapes a magnificent green while reducing roads to mud, flooding airstrips and complicating transfers to remote camps. Southern Africa may become hotter and drier, improving wildlife visibility around shrinking waterholes in the short term but placing animals, rivers and communities under increasing strain if drought persists. According to analysts, at Victoria Falls, reduced upstream rainfall could eventually reduce the thunderous curtain of water pouring over Victoria Falls, although the effect would be delayed by the vast size of the Zambezi catchment. Coral reefs are another major concern. The world has only recently emerged from the most extensive global bleaching event recorded, during which heat stress affected more than 80% of reef area â and further Pacific warming could expose already weakened reefs to another damaging season before they have had time to recover. Does El NiÃ±o mean the weather will be bad everywhere? No â and some destinations may experience conditions travellers actually consider favourable. The Caribbean could have fewer hurricanes, California ski resorts could receive substantial snowfall and drier weather may produce long stretches of sunshine across Indonesia. The danger lies in the point at which favourable weather becomes excessive â for example, with snow closing mountain roads, rain carrying away bridges crossing it, or sunshine becoming drought. Could El NiÃ±o affect safaris in Kenya or Tanzania? Quite possibly â and not necessarily for the worse. One of El NiÃ±oâs most consistent signatures is heavier short rains across East Africa between October and December. The East African savannah can look extraordinary after rain as dust settles and grasslands turn emerald green â with migratory birds arriving in huge numbers. Yet tracks that are easily navigable in August could become axle-deep mud by November, and small bush airstrips may temporarily close after particularly heavy downpours. During the 1997-98 El NiÃ±o, exceptionally heavy rain caused widespread flooding across East Africa, washing out roads and bridges in Kenya and leaving parts of the country difficult to reach. The most recent event offered another warning, as across Tanzania, the rains of 2023 and 2024 damaged 63 bridges, more than 800 kilometres of road and hundreds of culverts. Could El NiÃ±o affect the Maldives? The Maldives sits atop one of the worldâs most celebrated coral reef systems, making it one of the destinations most exposed to El NiÃ±oâs effects beneath the surface rather than above it. During the enormous 1997-98 event, sea temperatures rose so dramatically that large areas of coral across the Indian Ocean bleached, and scientists estimate that some Maldivian reefs lost more than 90 per cent of their shallow coral cover. The good news is that many reefs have since recovered remarkably well, but the bad news is that they are now entering another potential El NiÃ±o after enduring the most widespread global coral bleaching event ever recorded between 2023 and 2025. Marine life remains spectacular even on reefs that have experienced bleaching, but conditions may vary dramatically between atolls, and some reefs could face renewed stress if ocean temperatures climb significantly during late 2026 and early 2027. More widely, the Maldives may experience warmer seas, periods of unusual calm and changes in rainfall patterns, but it is unlikely to see the kind of extreme droughts or floods that could affect parts of Africa, South America or Southeast Asia. What could happen in Japan during El NiÃ±o? The country that first declared El NiÃ±oâs arrival may end up feeling relatively modest impacts compared with many tropical destinations. Historically, El NiÃ±o winters in Japan have tended to be warmer than average, which can be good news for city-break travellers exploring Tokyo, Kyoto or Osaka, but less welcome for ski resorts that are dependent on deep snowfall. The bigger concern for travellers may be summer heat. Japan has already experienced a succession of exceptionally hot summers in recent years, and El NiÃ±oâs tendency to boost global temperatures could make future heatwaves more intense. Could Thailand have a better winter than usual during El NiÃ±o? Thailand often sits on the drier side of El NiÃ±o, and during previous events, rainfall has decreased across much of the country while temperatures climbed higher than average â which means more reliable beach days in Phuket and Krabi and fewer interruptions to island-hopping itineraries. Yet there is another side to the story. The powerful 2015-16 El NiÃ±o contributed to one of Thailandâs most severe droughts in decades, with reservoirs reaching critically low levels and agricultural regions facing water shortages â so ultimately, what feels like perfect weather for a holiday can create serious challenges for the communities living through it. Should travellers to Bali and Indonesia be concerned? El NiÃ±o often brings Bali some of its most glorious weather: weeks of blue skies, lower humidity and uninterrupted sunsets. The problem is what can happen when the dry season refuses to end. The devastating Indonesian fire seasons of 1997-98 and 2015 were both closely linked to strong El NiÃ±o conditions, with vast areas of forest and peatland burned, producing smoke that spread across Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia. The smoke often originates hundreds of kilometres away, yet visitors can still feel the effects through disrupted flights and deteriorating air quality. Could El NiÃ±o affect European holidays? Europe sits far enough from the tropical Pacific that El NiÃ±oâs influence becomes considerably weaker and less predictable. However, strong El NiÃ±os often contribute to record global temperatures, and Europe has become increasingly prone to severe heatwaves regardless of what happens in the Pacific. The summer after the 1997-98 event was, at the time, the hottest year ever recorded globally, and the 2015â16 event helped produce another global temperature record. The most recent El NiÃ±o contributed to 2024 becoming the hottest year in modern measurements. Mediterranean destinations that were once comfortably warm in the shoulder seasons of June or September may increasingly become the sweet spot, while July and August edge further into heatwave territory. Could El NiÃ±o affect Mauritius, Seychelles and Zanzibar? During the 2016 bleaching episode in the Seychelles, between 69 and 99 per cent of coral was bleached at monitored locations, followed by an estimated 50 per cent reduction in hard coral cover â and another marine heatwave would affect those ecosystems as they recover from earlier damage. Mauritius has also experienced El NiÃ±o-related bleaching, including its first recorded mass event in 1998, although mortality was considerably lower at many sites than in the Seychelles. The 2023â24 El NiÃ±o, meanwhile, brought above-average rain to Tanzania across two successive rainy seasons, contributing to severe floods, landslides and extensive damage to roads and bridges.

item.title: Best pubs in Dublin: 13 drinking dens to visit on your next Irish city break
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
You’ve touched down in the Irish capital, and within hours you’re cocooned within the timeworn walls of one of the best pubs in Dublin, a ripped-open packet of Taytos and a pint of Guinness settling on the table in front of you. For many people, this is what a visit to the Irish capital is all about. Even better if a pair of musicians start to pluck and strum a few tunes in the corner as you fall into easy conversation with your fellow punters. I’ve spent many happy hours holed up in places on this list – whether quietly catching up with friends in the tucked-away snug in Kehoe’s or celebrating a big family birthday on a frosty December night at The Blue Light up in the Dublin Mountains. At a time when many pubs across rural Ireland are closing, it’s heartening to see new life being breathed into old-school boozers in the capital, proving that the Irish pub may be deeply rooted in tradition but its modern incarnation is ever-evolving. Here’s a pick of the best drinking dens in Dublin – from long-time favourites run by generations of the same family to revamped takes on the local watering hole. Best pub in Dublin for: new-look, old-school vibes The cosy interior of O’Reilly’s is actually the result of a 2025 renovation that kept the original wood-panelled pub feel but added an extra shine and pops of colour, including a red banquette and patinaed green wallpaper. The old apothecary bottles on display nod to the building’s former life as a chemist shop – as does the deco-esque shopfront – yet it’s only pints and good cheer being dispensed now. There’s live music on Friday and Saturday nights, and Bambino across the road slings pizza by the slice for post-pub munchies. This place might not have been on the radar before but its revamp is drawing in a new wave of curious customers. Address: O’Reilly’s, Merrion Row, Dublin D02 HY07 Best pub in Dublin for: an arty backdrop The darkly varnished walls of this always-buzzing spot are hung with abstract and colour-popping pieces by Irish artists, alongside a stained-glass panel depicting the pub’s interiors, down to the intricately patterned carpet. The crowd – more often than not sipping Grogan’s fine Guinness pour – spills out onto the terrace, which itself spills onto a pedestrianised street. The pub is particularly fun to visit at Christmas when every inch of space is bedecked in paintings for the annual art show; and Dublin expats are in town to catch up with old friends. Plus the no-frills toasties are legendary. Address: Grogan’s Castle Lounge, 15 South William Street, Dublin D02 H336 It’s hard to believe that this family-run pub in a beautiful red-brick building on George’s Street hasn’t been here for generations. Built on the site of much-hyped Rustic Stone restaurant, it has all the hallmarks of a timeless boozer; there are even open jam sessions on Sunday afternoons when anyone can come along and join the musicians. The first-floor dining room serves Carlingford oysters, burrata from County Cork buffaloes and dry-aged beef and Guinness stew, and on Sundays there’s a roast with all the trimmings. Some dishes come with vegetables from the chef’s own kitchen garden. A good spot for a feast with a gang of friends. Address: MJ Wright, 17 South Great George's Street, Dublin D02 HD76 Best pub in Dublin for: drinking with the locals One of the oldest and best pubs in Dublin, Mulligan’s was originally an illegal shebeen until it became licensed in 1782. It’s now run by a third generation of the Cusack family, and describes itself as a “no-nonsense pub with a cast of regulars and a lack of modern pomposity”. Interiors are creaking and characterful, and over the years punters who have graced its bar stools include James Joyce and John F. Kennedy, then working as a Hearst newspaper journalist (its links with the printed press are strong as The Irish Times offices were just over the road on D’Olier Street until they moved in 2005). Address: Mulligans, 8 Poolbeg Street, Dublin D02 TK71 In a prime location on a pedestrianised street off the main shopping drag, Grafton Street, brightly painted Kehoe’s (as it’s called locally) is the place to see Dublin street life play out. On a sunny day, punters spill out of the 220-year-old pub and sip pints beneath its blossoming flower baskets. On a cold winter’s day, the snug is the spot to bag, with a secret hatch to the bar and well-worn wooden benches. Friendly staff and a buzzy atmosphere make this a great spot for a post-shopping pit stop. Address: John Kehoe, 9 South Anne Street, Dublin D02 NY88 Best pub in Dublin for: a post-Temple Bar hideaway Temple Bar’s boisterous atmosphere can be a little overwhelming at times, even for the most seasoned carouser. So if you require something a little more authentic, say, head east on Fleet Street and look out for the old mounted clock in the distance. Bowes is a bit of a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it spot, but inside, it’s a warm and gregarious place with fine Guinness and even better craic. Opened in 1880, it has more than 200 bottles of whiskey on its wooden shelves, from American bourbons to Japanese single malts (the Irish Whiskey Society was founded here in 2009). Address: Bowes, 31 Fleet Street, Dublin D02 DF77 “A drinking pub with a music problem” goes the snappy tagline at The Cobblestone, but this is a friendly pub that takes its music seriously. And in a city with musicians proudly displaying their craft every night of the week, the journey from the city centre to the Cobblestone’s corner spot in the Smithfield area is well worth the trip. With superb musicians tapping out quality trad sessions to a receptive audience, this lively pub is built on respect for Irish culture – little wonder as owner Tom Mulligan’s family have been playing music for five generations. Address: The Cobblestone, 77 King Street North, Smithfield, Dublin D07 TP22 It’s a bit of a trip out of the city centre to the foothills of the Dublin Mountains, but The Blue Light’s terrace offers views of the city stretching as far as the hazy outline of the Howth peninsula. Dating back over 300 years, the pub takes its name from the ship’s light that signalled to smugglers that the coast was clear so they could safely land illegal rum, tobacco, wine and brandy. If you’ve been exploring the mountains or hiking the Wicklow Way, there’s no better spot for a post-walk pint; the cinematic views are at their best as the sun goes down and the city lights begin to flicker on. Just like those smugglers long ago, there’s still a feeling that you’re hiding out up here. Address: The Blue Light, Barnacullia, Sandyford, Dublin D18 PF72 John Fallon's “The Capstan Bar” Best pub in Dublin for: a post-whiskey tour pint In 2015, the first whiskey distilled in Dublin for almost 50 years passed through the Teeling Distillery in the historic Liberties district, and there’s nowhere better for a post-tour pint than the curiously named Capstan Bar. Just a five-minute walk from Teeling, this centuries-old street-corner pub in the shadow of St Patrick’s Cathedral pours some of the city’s finest Guinness. Grab the cosy snug if you’re lucky, and order a ham and cheese toastie made on Brennan’s batch bread, often served with a pot of mustard. Address: John Fallon’s, 129 The Coombe, The Liberties, Dublin D08 NP52 Best pub in Dublin for: literature nerds Writer James Joyce lived in European cities such as Paris, Zurich and Trieste, but his stories were almost always set in Dublin and one of the most vivid literary references to his hometown was at Davy Byrnes pub on Duke Street. Joyce himself drank here many times, and the main protagonist of his masterpiece Ulysses – Leopold Bloom – drops by the pub in chapter eight and orders a “gorgonzola sandwich and a glass of Burgundy”. Bloomsday, a joyous annual celebration of Joyce every 16 June, is particularly fun here. Address: Davy Byrnes, 21 Duke Street, Dublin D02 K380 John Kavanagh’s (aka ‘The Gravediggers’) Best pub in Dublin for: a peaceful pint of Guinness Is where to find the best Guinness the most subjective question of them all? There’s no doubt that Dublin is the finest city for the black stuff, but where it’s served is a whole different animal to ponder. With an evocative name and an even better drop of Guinness, John Kavanagh (aka The Gravediggers) in Glasnevin might be the pick of them all. Located next door to Glasnevin Cemetery (where many of Ireland’s most famous historic figures are buried) and dating back to 1833, it has an unfussy interior, and the lack of music and television means you can enjoy a peaceful pint. Order a bowl of traditional Dublin coddle when you’re here too. Address: John Kavanagh, 1 Prospect Square, Glasnevin, Dublin D09 CF72 From the Palace Bar to the Stag’s Head, Dublin is home to several lavishly decorated Victorian pubs, but few can match The Long Hall on South Great George’s Street. The red-and-white-striped awnings outside make it seem a little twee at first glance, but upon entering, it’s like stepping back in time to a glamorous 19th-century époque. Virtually unchanged since 1881, its cosy lounge is blanketed by a glossy crimson ceiling, with elaborate wooden partitions, antique clocks, globe lamps and red leather bar stools. The service here is excellent too, so settle in, order a pint and admire the splendour of one of Dublin’s great pubs. Address: The Long Hall, 51 South Great George's Street, Dublin D02 DV74 Best pub in Dublin for: musical heritage It’s only right that you’ll likely be greeted by raucous trad sounds swirling from inside the narrow old bar at O’Donoghues. Musical heritage runs deep here, with the Dubliners performing some of their earliest gigs within these walls in the 1960s. Black-and-white photos of that legendary band line the walls of this surprisingly capacious pub, with its airy courtyard, quieter second bar and upstairs space (though lead singer Ronnie Drew’s piercing blue eyes aren’t as vivid in sepia). There are rooms upstairs if you want to minimise the commute home. Address: O’Donoghue’s, 15 Merrion Row, Dublin D02 PF50

item.title: 17 Dreamy Hotels in Madrid Quietly Redefining Spanish Luxury
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Madrid is one of our favoriteÂ city breaks in Europe, beloved for its cultural landmarks, vivacious art scene, andÂ beautiful restaurants. These elements are also present within some of the best hotels in Madrid, where you can stay in historic palaces, art-gallery-meets-hotel hybrids, and unassuming addresses with Michelin-starred restaurants. Then there are the low-key stays, from new-gen hostels to apartment-style setups. And the scene is still growingâthe Four Seasons and Mandarin Oriental mark two of the newer luxury addresses in the Spanish capital. For the places to note ahead of your next visit, weâve rounded up the best hotels in Madrid below. Our top picks: - Best for a boutique stay: HÃ´tel du Temps Madrid - Read Full ReviewThe iconic Palace hotel in Madrid returned to its grande dame status in 2025 following a complete renovation by Ruiz Larrea Arquitectura, with LÃ¡zaro Rosa-ViolÃ¡n entrusted with the interiors. The end result is a beautiful love letter to Madrid. With 470 rooms and suites, The Palace is the largest luxury hotel in Madrid. The Neptuno Suite feels like stepping inside an elegant bourgeois Madrid house from the mid-20th century with its restored marble fireplace, wood paneling, Art Decoâinspired furniture, beautiful wallpaper above the headboards, and luxuries like Frette sheets and Le Chemin by Byredo bathroom amenities. Portuguese chef Nuno Matos has the task of breathing new life into La CÃºpula, which now more than ever is the social epicenter of the hotel. The menu is defined by its use of local produce, simple preparations, and embrace of tradition. Pork tenderloin with clam sauce, excellent cuts of meat, and a beef Wellington intended to be shared are classic dishes befitting a classic hotel. Cocktails were central to life at the original Palace, and the hotelâs bars remain committed to the classics, with some updates; drinks can be enjoyed not only at the bar in La CÃºpula, but also in the renovated and legendary bar, now called 27 Club. âD.M. - Read Full ReviewOne of the city's icons and a pioneer in luxury hospitality when it opened in 1886, the Gran Hotel InglÃ©s was the first hotel in Madrid to have a restaurant and electric lighting, as well as telephones and toilets with running water on each of its floorsâan extravagance for the time. Its 48 rooms and suites, designed with a nod to the Art Deco style, have bathtubs that were flown in from Canada and are custom-made for each room. The beds, meanwhile, come with 500-thread-count Egyptian cotton sheets and an extensive pillow menu. In addition to its signature cocktail and gastronomic offerings at Lobbyto, which serves Madrid cuisine with an avant-garde twist (donât miss the cocido madrileÃ±o!), the hotel has a brunch show with live music, an English tea service, and swing and rock-and-roll nights for the more lively. Le Max Club, the hotel's spa, includes a high-tech gym, spa cabins set up in collaboration with French brand Sisley (its botanical treatment menu is a delight, I promise), and a hot tub. âC.L. - Read Full ReviewMandarin Oriental knows that its Madrid outpost will forever be known simply as âThe Ritzââthe one inaugurated with pomp by King Alfonso XIII in 1910; the one that welcomed Grace Kelly and Rainier of Monaco during their honeymoon; and the one where Mata Hari, Salvador DalÃ, and countless other stars caroused. After its remodeling and reopening in 2021, The Ritz is now even more Ritz-like than ever, thanks to Mandarin Oriental. Storied Madrid architecture firm Rafael de La-Hoz and French interior designers Gilles & Boissier (whose touch graced the Baccarat Hotel New York) had the challenging task of reinventing the hotel while holding onto a certain spirit. The most striking detail was the recovery of the great glass vault of the Palm Court, the social heart of the building, which had been concealed for 80 years, and the opening of the enormous doors that connect, physicallyâand emotionallyâto the Museo del Prado (the great art gallery is so close you can almost touch it). But other magical corners abound. My favorites include The Beauty Concept spa, with its spectacular indoor pool, treatment cabins, and fitness trainers; the timeless counter of the Pictura cocktail bar, where Iâve spent endless hours watched over by gilt-framed oils; Deessa, chef Quique Dacostaâs artistic restaurant, which gained two Michelin stars in two years; and the rare oasis that is the hotel garden. To eat Dacostaâs paella here, under the cityâs eternal blue sky, has become a defining Madrid experience at what remains a quintessential hotel. âD.M. - Read Full ReviewSmack dab in the middle of Gran VÃa, Evok Collectionâs second opening outside France is leading the third hotel wave in the Spanish capitalâunsurprising given that one of the men who invented the boutique hotel helmed the design: Philippe Starck. The elegant, belvedere-topped seven-story building was finished in 1922. With the reception upstairs, the ground floor houses the bar, restaurant, and patisserie, which segue into each other, fostering a brasserie feel. The low-lit restaurant has woven-leather ceilings hung with double lampshades and mahogany-paneled walls. Chef Adam Bentalhaâs recipes roam the Med, from the Middle East (croissant-like challah; zaâatar-drenched suckling lamb shoulder) to the Iberian peninsula with Spanish produce (red tuna, Bellota ham). The 57 rooms and suites, a few with sun-trap terraces, have jatoba-wood joinery and are warmed by pinks and oranges, terra-cottas, and flashes of moss green. The La Capsule spa is decked with white and floaty curtains (very Delano Miami Ã la 1990s) and has a 65-foot pool clad in cream marble, a suite of biohacking gadgetry that includes a hyperbaric chamber, and a menu ranging from facial electrostimulation to Chinese massage. âLydia Bell - Read Full ReviewDesigned as a kind of contemporary bohemian retreat, NÃ´made Temple Madrid is structured around the idea of ââ"Halfway to Somewhere," which can be translated into a desire to foster encounters between travelers, artists, neighbors, creators, and the local community. There are 93 rooms and suitesâincluding two penthousesâwithin the hotel, all decorated with plenty of personality. Forget rustic minimalism: you'll find wallpaper, mirrors, brightly colored sheets, and vintage-inspired pieces mixed with bold contemporary silhouettes. The property is more than its rooms, thoughâguests can enjoy the rooftop bar and pool, a speakeasy and a nightclub, and carefully curated cultural programming at Monopol of the People, a versatile wellness and gathering space. In the basement, GÃN House of Healing spa is the picture of understated elegance and staffed by an outstanding team of therapists who will make you forget youâre in the heart of one of the worldâs most bustling cities. CafÃ© Libre, next to the eclectic and cozy lobby, is a space designed to make guests and visitors feel right at home. Itâs the perfect spot to enjoy some tapas, a few beers, or a light bite, right on the street level. âClara Laguna - Read Full ReviewFor over a century, the Edificio MetrÃ³polisâmuch photographed and admired but for years elusively inaccessibleâhas defined Madridâs skyline. Now, a distinct and ambitious renovation project, stewarded by Marta Seco and Sandro Silvaâs Grupo Paraguas, has restored not only its architectural splendor but also its vital pulse. Reborn as Club MetrÃ³polis, the landmark buildingâs eight floors now house an international private members club, a 19-room boutique hotel, and seven restaurants, and are set to host a roster of twice-weekly experiences. Hotel guests enjoy club membership and all-area access for the duration of their stay. LÃ¡zaro Rosa-ViolÃ¡nâs design brings coherence to the interiors, shaping the building as a single contemporary house where luxury lies in discretion and a sense of belonging and time shared. From the surprising Spa de Langostas restaurant to the rooftop overlooking the city, and from the intimacy of the rooms to La GalerÃaâs languid mood, Club MetrÃ³polis comes together as a new way to experience Madrid. âMarÃa Casbas - Read Full ReviewHÃ´tel du Temps Madrid is born of Yoan and Jen Marciano, creators of the legendary HÃ´tel du Temps in Paris, who decided to start a new life in the Spanish capital with their children. It was love at first sight with this building in MalasaÃ±a, and after eight months of renovating a former hotel right on Calle Barco, almost at the corner of Gran VÃa and with the TelefÃ³nica building watching over it, the Marcianos opened HÃ´tel du Temps Madrid. There are 31 rooms in total, 7 of them suites with living rooms and large windows or even small terraces overlooking the street. The jewel of the house is the rooftop suite, a kind of detached cottage with a private terrace where the silence is resounding, even though you are just steps away from Gran VÃa, the second busiest shopping street in Europe. All rooms feature amenities created for the hotel by perfumer Francisca Manzini in collaboration with the Marciano family. Comfort and warmth abound, with a retro atmosphere that permeates everything. On the rooftop is a plunge pool where guests can cool off and enjoy a drink while soaking during Madridâs sweltering summer months. âDavid Moralejo - Read Full ReviewTucked away in the refined ChamberÃ neighbourhood, Hotel Orfila is a 19th-century palace radiating old Spanish glamour. With just 32 rooms and suites, this intimate Relais & ChÃ¢teaux property feels more like a private residence than a hotel, with its aristocratic wallpapers, shiny silverware, portrait-lined corridors, and the gentle scent of fine soap drifting through the halls. The undisputed highlight is breakfast: an exceptional spread of cured meats, quince paste, and sourdough, elevated further by churros con chocolate served Ã la carte. In warmer months, the tiered garden terrace transforms this into one of Madrid's most civilized morning rituals. Service is impeccably formal yet quietly warm, with a concierge well-versed in securing restaurant reservations, museum tickets, and local experiences. The location is perfectly placed for access to the Prado, Retiro Park, and the unmissable Sorolla Museum. And with violet sweets left on the pillow each evening, Orfila feels unapologetically, gloriously old-school. âStuart Brumfitt - Read Full ReviewPerfectly positioned between the vibrant Madrid neighborhoods of MalasaÃ±a and Chueca, 7 Islas is a quietly cool boutique hotel just two blocks from the Gran VÃa. The hotel has a minimalist aesthetic, with polished concrete floors, rotating contemporary artwork, and considered design details, but itâs totally relaxed and welcoming. The best rooms here are the spacious loft-style Ãtico rooms with private terraces and sweeping rooftop views, ideal for warm Madrid evenings. Expect Malin+Goetz toiletries, Technogym fitness facilities, and welcome daiquiris on arrival. A comprehensive morning breakfast buffet and quiet cocktail bar complete the in-house offerings. The real strength here is the service: a well-connected team able to secure hard-to-book restaurant reservations, sold-out football tickets, and bespoke experiences, from exclusive cigar clubs to private cultural encounters. Family-friendly, eco-conscious, and genuinely characterful, 7 Islas punches well above its price point. âS.B. - Read Full ReviewThe MeliÃ¡ Collection opened its first hotel in Madrid, Casa de las Artes, with the aim of redefining luxury through a focus on modernity, art, and culture. Located in the Barrio de las Letras, the hotel is in a Beaux Artsâstyle building that once housed the General Association of Railway Employees. Inside, original DalÃ lithographs decorate the walls, and a midcentury corridor leads to an indoor swimming pool and creatively designed meeting rooms. The 137 rooms include unique illustrations of Don Quixote, warm furnishings, Nespresso machines, and luxury bath products by Carner. The hotel's restaurant, MachÃ©, serves classic Madrid tapas alongside a variety of fish and meats, while a cozy cinema named MirÃ³ pays tribute to the private projection rooms of Hollywoodâs Golden Age. âD.M. - Read Full ReviewFor years, MadrileÃ±os avoided the streets around Puerta del Sol, complaining about the decay of a once-grand downtown barrio that had also become a monstrous building site. But since the Four Seasons opened its doors in September 2020, those complaints have turned to compliments. Standing proudly on the corner of calles Sevilla and AlcalÃ¡, the Canadian groupâs first Spanish property has sailed onto the Madrid hotel scene with all guns blazing, promising to grant the neighborhood a new lease on life. Part of a large project including private residences, a retail "gallery," and a gastro-market, the hotel has preserved the buildingâs ornate 19th-century stone faÃ§ade (check out the elephant heads) and grand interiors such as the double-height lobby with its ivy-green marble columns, Alpujarra carpets, and stained-glass roof. You wonât find cutting-edge here, but there are no rough edges either: this is grown-up stuff. Everything breathes quality, from the solid walnut floors and gray-flecked Volakas marble of the rooms to the faultless soundproofing and refreshingly user-friendly lighting systems. Service manages the deft trick of being both briskly efficient and charmingly Spanish. In the top-floor restaurant, chef Dani Garcia does his New Andalusian thing to fabulous backdrop views of monumental Madrid. The Four Seasons sets the bar high, but clears it without breaking a sweat. âP.R. - Read Full ReviewThe drama of the Madrid Edition buildingâcunningly repurposed from a boxy former bank HQ on the old-town Plaza de Celenqueâbegins with the ornate 18th-century granite doorway by Pedro de Rivera (one of the few historic elements remaining from the original site) and continues into a vast spiral staircase in pearly-white stone, curving spectacularly upwards like a giant seashell. The public spaces have a low-lit calm but go all-out for contrast: An antique tapestry hangs behind an all-white pool table lined with electric-blue baize, and you might find a minimalist bench artfully draped with a traditional Spanish shawl. On the ground floor, chef Enrique Olvera disembarks from Mexico City with a restaurant (JerÃ³nimo) that eschews fancy fine dining for a streamlined modern interpretation of traditional Mexican cuisine; if budgetary restrictions apply, an evening in the Edition's rooftop wonderland is another great way of catching the hotelâs hedonistic vibe. âPaul Richardson - Read Full ReviewThe raison d'Ãªtre of JW Marriott Hotel Madrid comes from the founder of the brand (as well as the larger Marriott Corporation), J. Willard Marriott, who firmly believed in the importance of personalized service. Wherever you look and wherever you go on the property, there's the opportunity to check out of real life and embrace the present. A carpe diem attitude is expressed in elegantly pared-back rooms in neutral colors and attentive staff. The hotelâs restaurant is its crown jewel, the creation of the celebrated Sandoval brothers. Expect local produce and traditional meets cutting-edge cooking (plus, I'd say, the best breakfast in Europe). Service is endearingly enthusiastic, and the public spaces (cocktail bar, lobby, bookstore) make this the capital's trendiest spot right now.âMarÃa Ãngeles Cano - Read Full ReviewBasing yourself at Rosewoodâs first Spanish property in Madridâs upscale Salamanca quarter is like staying just off Fifth Avenue in New Yorkâyouâll think the city is all designer boutiques and people in gilets if you donât wander further afield. The vibe inside is very local and knowingâblack-framed floor-to-ceiling glass doors, tongue-in-cheek artworks smuggled among more serious pieces, and smart lounges you no longer have to book a table at. Regular restaurant pop-ups are intricate and designed to entice Madridâs curious foodies, while the on-site patisserie Flor y Nata casts intoxicating smells. All-day dining destination Las Brasas de Castellana serves wonderful traditional dishes, and flagship AmÃ³s, run by three-Michelin-star-winning JesÃºs SÃ¡nchez, does skillful creative turns on Northern Spanish cuisine. Underground, thereâs a small, stylish spa with a uniquely shaped hot tub, plus a sauna and steam room; up top is the last piece of the puzzleâthe show-stopping Houses opened in 2022. Ask for Royal Anglada House for a seemingly endless space stretching over a long dining room, circular office, and both indoor and outdoor kitchens, the latter on a wow-worthy terrace with views out to the mountains beyond the cityscape. âBecky Lucas FAQ: Which part of Madrid is the best to stay in? Many of Madrid's hotels are conveniently scattered around Centro, the city's central area. To be smack-dab in the thick of it, look to addresses surrounding the busy Gran VÃa or the Literary Quarter of Barrio de las Letras. For a stay that's outside the hustle and bustle, head to the glamorous and grand boulevards of Salamanca where you'll find smart yet unassuming boltholes likeÂ Rosewood Villa Magna and Hotel Ãnico Madrid. Every hotel review on this list has been written by a CondÃ© Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.
